### On a server

Three ports, and only the first needs to be memorable:
**The relay is not an HTTP service, and only one of its three listeners can be proxied.**
Signalling is a WebSocket and nginx can front it. Control is a raw TCP splice carrying a TLS session
belonging to the two ends — nginx's `sites-enabled` cannot proxy it, and neither can anything else
that expects HTTP. Video is UDP. So the shape depends on whether the machine already serves HTTPS.

| Port | Protocol | What |
| Port | Protocol | Proxied? |
|---|---|---|
| 443 | TCP | Signalling. 443 rather than something free, because it is the one port guest and corporate networks nev
er block |
| 9443 | TCP | Control relay |
| 40000–40100 | UDP | Video, one port per live session |
| signalling | TCP | Yes, if you want — see B |
| control | TCP | **No.** Direct only |
| video | UDP | **No.** Direct only |

**DNS** — an `A` record for the relay host pointing at the server. Add an `AAAA` too if it has IPv6,
and check which the clients actually pick, because a broken IPv6 route shows up as a connection
that hangs rather than one that fails.
**DNS** — an `A` record for the relay host. Add an `AAAA` if the server has IPv6, and check which one
clients actually pick: a broken IPv6 route shows up as a connection that hangs rather than one that
fails, which is much harder to diagnose.

**Firewall** — open exactly the three above and nothing else. The video rule can only be written
once `PEERINGD_VIDEO_PORTS` is set.
#### A — direct ports

Simplest, and right for a machine with nothing else on it. The relay owns its ports and terminates
its own TLS.

```ini
Environment=PEERINGD_SIGNAL_ADDR=0.0.0.0:8443
Environment=PEERINGD_CONTROL_ADDR=0.0.0.0:9443
Environment=PEERINGD_VIDEO_PORTS=40000-40100
Environment=PEERINGD_TLS_CERT=/etc/letsencrypt/live/peering.dmqq.dev/fullchain.pem
Environment=PEERINGD_TLS_KEY=/etc/letsencrypt/live/peering.dmqq.dev/privkey.pem
```

Bind 443 if it is free — it is the one port guest and corporate networks never block. Otherwise use
anything, accepting that a restrictive network may refuse it.

#### B — nginx in front of signalling

For a machine already serving HTTPS, where 443 is taken. nginx terminates TLS for the WebSocket and
the relay does not need a certificate at all.

```nginx
server {
    listen 443 ssl http2;
    listen [::]:443 ssl http2;
    server_name peering.dmqq.dev;

    ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/peering.dmqq.dev/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/peering.dmqq.dev/privkey.pem;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8443;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

        # Not optional. A Mac that is registered holds this socket open and says nothing for
        # minutes at a time, and nginx closes an idle proxied connection at 60 seconds. Drop it
        # and the Mac looks offline to every phone, intermittently, for no visible reason.
        proxy_read_timeout 1h;
        proxy_send_timeout 1h;
    }
}
```

```ini
Environment=PEERINGD_SIGNAL_ADDR=127.0.0.1:8443
Environment=PEERINGD_CONTROL_ADDR=0.0.0.0:9443
Environment=PEERINGD_VIDEO_PORTS=40000-40100

# Required here, and the one setting that is easy to miss. Without it the relay reports the address
# each client reached it on as the place to connect for control and video — which is right when
# clients address it directly, and behind nginx is 127.0.0.1, so every client would be told to
# connect to itself.
Environment=PEERINGD_PUBLIC_HOST=peering.dmqq.dev
```

The relay's signalling listener stays on loopback; nginx is the only thing that reaches it. Control
and video are opened directly in the firewall and are **not** proxied.

#### Firewall

Open exactly the ports in use and nothing else:

```sh
certbot certonly --standalone -d peering.dmqq.dev
# shape A
ufw allow 8443/tcp && ufw allow 9443/tcp && ufw allow 40000:40100/udp
# shape B
ufw allow 443/tcp  && ufw allow 9443/tcp && ufw allow 40000:40100/udp
```

The video rule can only be written once `PEERINGD_VIDEO_PORTS` is set.

#### Unit, and updating

```ini
[Unit]
Description=Peering relay


[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/peeringd
Environment=PEERINGD_SIGNAL_ADDR=0.0.0.0:443
Environment=PEERINGD_CONTROL_ADDR=0.0.0.0:9443
Environment=PEERINGD_VIDEO_PORTS=40000-40100
Environment=PEERINGD_TLS_CERT=/etc/letsencrypt/live/peering.dmqq.dev/fullchain.pem
Environment=PEERINGD_TLS_KEY=/etc/letsencrypt/live/peering.dmqq.dev/privkey.pem
EnvironmentFile=/etc/peeringd.env
Environment=RUST_LOG=info
Restart=always
# Binding 443 as a non-root user needs this, and it is narrower than running the relay as root.
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
User=peering

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

Only signalling needs a certificate, and only so the token exchange is not readable in transit —
the media is encrypted end to end regardless and does not depend on it. Binding 443 as a normal user
needs `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`, which is preferable to running a network-facing service as root.
`Environment=` lines go in `/etc/peeringd.env`, which keeps the unit readable and the settings
greppable. Binding 443 directly needs `AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`; shape B does not,
since nginx owns that port.

**Updating.** The binary is static and has no runtime dependencies, so an update is a file
replacement and a restart:
The binary is static with no runtime dependencies, so an update is a file replacement:

```sh
systemctl stop peeringd

ssh server 'chmod +x /usr/local/bin/peeringd && systemctl start peeringd'
```

Restarting drops live sessions, and the two ends reconnect on their own — the Mac re-registers and
the phone asks again. Worth doing when nobody is mid-session anyway.
Restarting drops live sessions and both ends reconnect on their own — the Mac re-registers, the
phone asks again. Worth doing when nobody is mid-session anyway.

#### One limitation worth knowing

Shape B gets signalling onto 443, but **control still needs 9443**. Some corporate and hotel
networks allow only 80 and 443 outbound, so the app will find the Mac and then fail to open the
control connection. Cellular and home networks are unaffected, which covers the intended use, but
it is a real edge and worth recognising from the symptom rather than debugging from scratch.

Bandwidth is the only real running cost: see the note below.

┌────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Listener  │                  Protocol                  │            Can nginx front it?             │
├────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ signalling │ WebSocket                                  │ Yes — this is the one                      │
├────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤

├────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ video      │ UDP                                        │ No                                         │
└────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────┘

So your shape is: nginx terminates TLS on 443 for the WebSocket, and control and video are opened directly on their own ports. The relay keeps its signalling listener on loopback where only nginx reaches it — it doesn't need a certificate at all in that arrangement, since nginx has one.

Added 51 lines
The relay's signalling listener stays on loopback; nginx is the only thing that reaches it. Control
and video are opened directly in the firewall and are **not** proxied.

#### Behind Cloudflare

**Cloudflare's proxy carries HTTP and HTTPS and nothing else.** It proxies a fixed list of ports —
443, 8443 and a handful of others — and it does not proxy UDP at all outside Spectrum, which is
priced for enterprises rather than for this. So of the relay's three listeners, Cloudflare can
carry exactly one: signalling.

That has a consequence that is easy to miss and unpleasant to debug: **the name in
`PEERINGD_PUBLIC_HOST` must not be proxied.** Clients open control and video against that name, and
if it has the orange cloud they will be sent to Cloudflare, which will drop the connection because
9443 is not a port it proxies and UDP is not traffic it carries. What that looks like from the app
is signalling working perfectly and the session never opening — which reads as a relay bug rather
than a DNS setting.

So use two names:

| Name | Cloudflare | Carries |
|---|---|---|
| `peering.dmqq.dev` | Proxied (orange) | Signalling only. Cloudflare → nginx → the relay's loopback listener |
| something like `relay.dmqq.dev` | **DNS only (grey)** | Control and video. Clients reach the server directly |

```
PEERINGD_PUBLIC_HOST=relay.dmqq.dev
```

Signalling still benefits from the orange cloud: the WebSocket rides HTTPS on 443, which is the one
port nothing blocks.

#### IPv6

Worth being deliberate about, because a proxied name hides the problem and the direct ports cannot.

**Bind dual-stack if the server is IPv6.** The defaults are `0.0.0.0`, which is IPv4 only. On a
server whose clients arrive over IPv6, set:

```
PEERINGD_SIGNAL_ADDR=127.0.0.1:8443
PEERINGD_CONTROL_ADDR=[::]:9443
PEERINGD_VIDEO_BIND=[::]:0
```

`[::]` accepts IPv4 as well on Linux, where `net.ipv6.bindv6only` is 0 by default, so this covers
both.

**A grey-cloud name pointing only at IPv6 will not work for IPv4-only clients.** Cloudflare's proxy
hides that for HTTP — it terminates the connection and reaches your origin however it can — but
control and video go straight to the origin, so a client on an IPv4-only network simply cannot reach
them. Polish fixed-line and much of mobile is IPv6-reachable, so this may be fine in practice, but
it is the thing to know before wondering why one particular network never connects. An `A` record
alongside the `AAAA` removes the question entirely.

Then Cloudflare carries exactly one of the relay's three listeners, and it fails in a way that looks like a relay bug rather than a DNS setting.

Cloudflare's proxy handles HTTP/HTTPS on a fixed list of ports — 9443 isn't on it — and carries no UDP at all outside Spectrum, which is enterprise pricing. So signalling rides the orange cloud fine as a WebSocket on 443, and control and video can never go through it.

The trap is PEERINGD_PUBLIC_HOST. That's the name clients are told to open control and video against. If it's your orange-cloud name, every client gets sent to Cloudflare, which drops the connection. From the app that looks like signalling working perfectly and the session never opening. So you need two names:

┌─────────────────────┬──────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│        Name         │    Cloudflare    │                      Carries                       │
├─────────────────────┼──────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ peering.dmqq.dev    │ proxied (orange) │ signalling: Cloudflare → nginx → relay on loopback │
├─────────────────────┼──────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ e.g. relay.dmqq.dev │ DNS only (grey)  │ control + video, straight to the server            │
└─────────────────────┴──────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

PEERINGD_PUBLIC_HOST=relay.dmqq.dev

Now the question that might actually block you: does that box have an IPv4 address, or is it IPv6-only?

If it's IPv6-only, Cloudflare hides that for HTTP — it terminates the connection and reaches your origin however it can — but control and video go direct to the origin. A phone on an IPv4-only network can't reach them at all, and you'd get exactly the same silent symptom: signalling connects, session never opens. An A record alongside the AAAA removes the question entirely, and is worth having even if IPv6 usually works.

Two related things while you're in the config:

- The defaults bind 0.0.0.0, which is IPv4-only. On an IPv6 server set PEERINGD_CONTROL_ADDR=[::]:9443 and PEERINGD_VIDEO_BIND=[::]:0 — [::] accepts both families on Linux, since bindv6only is 0 by default.
- Everything in the README's shape B already assumes nginx terminates TLS, which is what you want behind Cloudflare — the relay doesn't need a certificate there at all.

`[::]` accepts IPv4 as well on Linux, where `net.ipv6.bindv6only` is 0 by default, so this covers
both.

**A grey-cloud name pointing only at IPv6 will not work for IPv4-only clients.** Cloudflare's proxy
hides that for HTTP — it terminates the connection and reaches your origin however it can — but
control and video go straight to the origin, so a client on an IPv4-only network simply cannot reach
them. Polish fixed-line and much of mobile is IPv6-reachable, so this may be fine in practice, but
it is the thing to know before wondering why one particular network never connects. An `A` record
alongside the `AAAA` removes the question entirely.
**An IPv6-only server is a real limitation, and it constrains both ends.** Cloudflare's proxy hides
the problem for signalling — it terminates the connection and reaches the origin however it can, so
a dual-stack edge covers an IPv6-only origin. But control and video go straight to the origin, so
*both* the phone and the Mac must have IPv6 to open a session. The Mac matters more than the phone,
and is easier to overlook: it is the end that has to be reachable at all times, from whatever
network it happens to be sitting on.

What it looks like when it fails is signalling connecting, the host appearing online, and the
session never opening — on some networks and not others, which reads as flakiness rather than as a
missing address family.

Three ways out, in the order worth trying:

1. **Buy an IPv4 address.** Most providers that offer IPv6-only instances sell an IPv4 for a small
   monthly fee — around €0.50 at the common European hosts. This is by far the cheapest fix, and it
   is a line on a bill rather than a piece of architecture. Check the provider's console before
   designing around the absence.
2. **Move the relay to a dual-stack host.** The relay is a 4 MB static binary with no runtime
   dependencies; it has no attachment to any particular machine.
3. **Accept IPv6-only and be explicit about it.** Legitimate for a personal tool used from networks
   you control, and worth stating plainly in the app rather than leaving users to infer it from a
   session that will not open.

Cloudflare Spectrum can proxy arbitrary TCP and UDP and would solve this, but it is priced for
enterprises and is not a reasonable line item for this product.

Right — so let me be straight about what that costs you, because it's more than it looks.

Cloudflare covers your signalling and nothing else. Its edge is dual-stack, so it accepts the phone's and Mac's connections over IPv4 and reaches your IPv6-only origin however it can. But control and video go straight to the origin, so both ends need IPv6 to open a session.

The Mac is the one that matters and the one that's easy to miss. It's the end that has to be reachable from wherever it happens to be sitting, at all times — that's the entire product. An IPv6-only origin quietly excludes every IPv4-only network the Mac might land on: a hotel, an office, a friend's house, some fraction of Polish ISPs. And the symptom is the nasty one again — signalling connects, the host shows as online, the session never opens — except now it's network-dependent, so it presents as flakiness rather than as a
missing address family.

      # peeringd
      
      The relay that lets a phone reach its Mac from outside the local network.
      
      Both ends sit behind NATs that will not admit unsolicited traffic, so both connect *outward* to
      this process. It introduces them, splices their control connections, and forwards their video
      datagrams. Neither end ever learns the other's address, because neither end needs to — both
      address the relay.
      
      ## What it does not do
      
      **It cannot read anything it carries.** Control is a TLS session belonging to the two ends, which
      the relay copies without terminating. Video is sealed with a key the two ends exchanged over that
      TLS session, and which the relay was never told. Its tokens are addressing hints, not credentials.
      
      That property is the product. "Your Mac's screen does not pass through our servers in a form we can
      see" has to stay true as this code grows, and the way to keep it true is to keep this process too
      stupid to break it. If a change here would let the relay inspect, alter, or authorize traffic, the
      change is wrong.
      
      A consequence worth understanding: **anyone who learns a Mac's device ID can ask the relay to open
      a pipe to it.** That is deliberate. The relay is not the thing that grants access — the TLS
      handshake and the pin are, and someone who knows the ID gets a pipe and then fails the handshake.
      Having the Mac hand its paired-device list to the relay would let it refuse earlier, at the cost of
      giving the server a map of who is paired with whom. Silence is the better trade.
      
      ## Running it
      
      ```sh
      cargo run                       # loopback: signalling on :8443, control on :9443
      cargo run --release             # same, optimised
      cargo test                      # 30 unit tests and 5 end-to-end socket tests
      ```
      
      With no configuration it listens on all interfaces, picks a video port per session, and serves
      signalling in plaintext. That is exactly right for pointing both apps at `127.0.0.1`, and never
      right for a public address.
      
      | Variable | Default | Meaning |
      |---|---|---|
      | `PEERINGD_SIGNAL_ADDR` | `0.0.0.0:8443` | Signalling listener |
      | `PEERINGD_CONTROL_ADDR` | `0.0.0.0:9443` | Control relay listener |
      | `PEERINGD_VIDEO_BIND` | `0.0.0.0:0` | Address per-session UDP sockets bind to |
      | `PEERINGD_VIDEO_PORTS` | — | Range session video ports come from, e.g. `40000-40100`. **Set this anywhere with a firewall** — see below |
      | `PEERINGD_TLS_CERT` | — | Certificate for signalling. Both this and the key, or neither |
      | `PEERINGD_TLS_KEY` | — | Private key for signalling |
      | `PEERINGD_SESSION_TTL` | `300` | Seconds a session survives without activity |
      
      **`PEERINGD_VIDEO_PORTS` matters more than it looks.** Unset, the OS picks each session's video
      port from the whole ephemeral range — 32768 to 60999 on a default Linux — so allowing video through
      a firewall means opening twenty-eight thousand UDP ports. A range of a hundred turns that into one
      rule. What a closed range looks like is *control working and video never arriving*, which is a
      miserable thing to debug from the symptom; the startup log prints the range that will be used so it
      can be checked against the firewall directly.
      
      The relay reports the address a client reached it on as the address to connect back to, so a
      directly-addressed server needs no configuration for this. `RUST_LOG=debug` for per-connection
      detail; `info` shows registrations and session allocations.
      
      ### On a server
      
      **The relay is not an HTTP service, and only one of its three listeners can be proxied.**
      Signalling is a WebSocket and nginx can front it. Control is a raw TCP splice carrying a TLS session
      belonging to the two ends — nginx's `sites-enabled` cannot proxy it, and neither can anything else
      that expects HTTP. Video is UDP. So the shape depends on whether the machine already serves HTTPS.
      
      | Port | Protocol | Proxied? |
      |---|---|---|
      | signalling | TCP | Yes, if you want — see B |
      | control | TCP | **No.** Direct only |
      | video | UDP | **No.** Direct only |
      
      **DNS** — an `A` record for the relay host. Add an `AAAA` if the server has IPv6, and check which one
      clients actually pick: a broken IPv6 route shows up as a connection that hangs rather than one that
      fails, which is much harder to diagnose.
      
      #### A — direct ports
      
      Simplest, and right for a machine with nothing else on it. The relay owns its ports and terminates
      its own TLS.
      
      ```ini
      Environment=PEERINGD_SIGNAL_ADDR=0.0.0.0:8443
      Environment=PEERINGD_CONTROL_ADDR=0.0.0.0:9443
      Environment=PEERINGD_VIDEO_PORTS=40000-40100
      Environment=PEERINGD_TLS_CERT=/etc/letsencrypt/live/peering.dmqq.dev/fullchain.pem
      Environment=PEERINGD_TLS_KEY=/etc/letsencrypt/live/peering.dmqq.dev/privkey.pem
      ```
      
      Bind 443 if it is free — it is the one port guest and corporate networks never block. Otherwise use
      anything, accepting that a restrictive network may refuse it.
      
      #### B — nginx in front of signalling
      
      For a machine already serving HTTPS, where 443 is taken. nginx terminates TLS for the WebSocket and
      the relay does not need a certificate at all.
      
      ```nginx
      server {
          listen 443 ssl http2;
          listen [::]:443 ssl http2;
          server_name peering.dmqq.dev;
      
          ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/peering.dmqq.dev/fullchain.pem;
          ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/peering.dmqq.dev/privkey.pem;
      
          location / {
              proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8443;
              proxy_http_version 1.1;
              proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
              proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
              proxy_set_header Host $host;
              proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
              proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
              proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
      
              # Not optional. A Mac that is registered holds this socket open and says nothing for
              # minutes at a time, and nginx closes an idle proxied connection at 60 seconds. Drop it
              # and the Mac looks offline to every phone, intermittently, for no visible reason.
              proxy_read_timeout 1h;
              proxy_send_timeout 1h;
          }
      }
      ```
      
      ```ini
      Environment=PEERINGD_SIGNAL_ADDR=127.0.0.1:8443
      Environment=PEERINGD_CONTROL_ADDR=0.0.0.0:9443
      Environment=PEERINGD_VIDEO_PORTS=40000-40100
      
      # Required here, and the one setting that is easy to miss. Without it the relay reports the address
      # each client reached it on as the place to connect for control and video — which is right when
      # clients address it directly, and behind nginx is 127.0.0.1, so every client would be told to
      # connect to itself.
      Environment=PEERINGD_PUBLIC_HOST=peering.dmqq.dev
      ```
      
      The relay's signalling listener stays on loopback; nginx is the only thing that reaches it. Control
      and video are opened directly in the firewall and are **not** proxied.
      
      #### Behind Cloudflare
      
      **Cloudflare's proxy carries HTTP and HTTPS and nothing else.** It proxies a fixed list of ports —
      443, 8443 and a handful of others — and it does not proxy UDP at all outside Spectrum, which is
      priced for enterprises rather than for this. So of the relay's three listeners, Cloudflare can
      carry exactly one: signalling.
      
      That has a consequence that is easy to miss and unpleasant to debug: **the name in
      `PEERINGD_PUBLIC_HOST` must not be proxied.** Clients open control and video against that name, and
      if it has the orange cloud they will be sent to Cloudflare, which will drop the connection because
      9443 is not a port it proxies and UDP is not traffic it carries. What that looks like from the app
      is signalling working perfectly and the session never opening — which reads as a relay bug rather
      than a DNS setting.
      
      So use two names:
      
      | Name | Cloudflare | Carries |
      |---|---|---|
      | `peering.dmqq.dev` | Proxied (orange) | Signalling only. Cloudflare → nginx → the relay's loopback listener |
      | something like `relay.dmqq.dev` | **DNS only (grey)** | Control and video. Clients reach the server directly |
      
      ```
      PEERINGD_PUBLIC_HOST=relay.dmqq.dev
      ```
      
      Signalling still benefits from the orange cloud: the WebSocket rides HTTPS on 443, which is the one
      port nothing blocks.
      
      #### IPv6
      
      Worth being deliberate about, because a proxied name hides the problem and the direct ports cannot.
      
      **Bind dual-stack if the server is IPv6.** The defaults are `0.0.0.0`, which is IPv4 only. On a
      server whose clients arrive over IPv6, set:
      
      ```
      PEERINGD_SIGNAL_ADDR=127.0.0.1:8443
      PEERINGD_CONTROL_ADDR=[::]:9443
      PEERINGD_VIDEO_BIND=[::]:0
      ```
      
      `[::]` accepts IPv4 as well on Linux, where `net.ipv6.bindv6only` is 0 by default, so this covers
      both.
      
      **An IPv6-only server is a real limitation, and it constrains both ends.** Cloudflare's proxy hides
      the problem for signalling — it terminates the connection and reaches the origin however it can, so
      a dual-stack edge covers an IPv6-only origin. But control and video go straight to the origin, so
      *both* the phone and the Mac must have IPv6 to open a session. The Mac matters more than the phone,
      and is easier to overlook: it is the end that has to be reachable at all times, from whatever
      network it happens to be sitting on.
      
      What it looks like when it fails is signalling connecting, the host appearing online, and the
      session never opening — on some networks and not others, which reads as flakiness rather than as a
      missing address family.
      
      Three ways out, in the order worth trying:
      
      1. **Buy an IPv4 address.** Most providers that offer IPv6-only instances sell an IPv4 for a small
         monthly fee — around €0.50 at the common European hosts. This is by far the cheapest fix, and it
         is a line on a bill rather than a piece of architecture. Check the provider's console before
         designing around the absence.
      2. **Move the relay to a dual-stack host.** The relay is a 4 MB static binary with no runtime
         dependencies; it has no attachment to any particular machine.
      3. **Accept IPv6-only and be explicit about it.** Legitimate for a personal tool used from networks
         you control, and worth stating plainly in the app rather than leaving users to infer it from a
         session that will not open.
      
      Cloudflare Spectrum can proxy arbitrary TCP and UDP and would solve this, but it is priced for
      enterprises and is not a reasonable line item for this product.
      
      #### Shared IPv4 with forwarded ports
      
      Some hosts — mikr.us among them — give you a public IPv6 address and no IPv4 of your own, but
      forward a handful of ports on a shared IPv4 address. **That is enough, and it needs only two of
      them**, because signalling rides Cloudflare and never touches IPv4 directly:
      
      | Forwarded port | To | Carries |
      |---|---|---|
      | one TCP | the relay's control port | Control |
      | one UDP | the relay's video port | Video |
      
      **This shape needs two names**, and the reason is the one above: a hostname is either proxied or
      not, and control and video cannot be proxied.
      
      | Name | Cloudflare | Points at | Carries |
      |---|---|---|---|
      | `peering.dmqq.dev` | proxied | nginx | Signalling |
      | `relay.dmqq.dev` | **DNS only** | the shared IPv4 | Control and video |
      
      ```
      PEERINGD_VIDEO_PORTS=40000-40000
      PEERINGD_PUBLIC_HOST=relay.dmqq.dev
      ```
      
      **The forwarded port need not match the bound one**, and it usually does not on a shared address —
      the host picks both. Only the outside number is reachable, so tell the relay which it is:
      
      ```
      PEERINGD_CONTROL_ADDR=[::]:9443
      PEERINGD_PUBLIC_CONTROL_PORT=51234    # what mikr.us forwards to 9443
      
      PEERINGD_PUBLIC_VIDEO_PORT=51235      # what mikr.us forwards to 40000
      ```
      
      Both default to the bound port, so they are only needed when the two differ. Check the forwarding
      panel before assuming; getting it wrong produces clients that are told to connect to a port that
      nothing answers on, which looks exactly like the relay being down.
      
      **The video range must be as small as the number of ports you forward** — with one forwarded UDP
      port, a single-port range. The relay refuses a session when its range is exhausted rather than
      quietly sharing a port, so a range wider than the forwarding is a session that cannot start rather
      than two sessions that interfere.
      
      One port is genuinely enough for this product: one phone, one Mac, one session. A reconnect
      supersedes the previous session and takes the port straight back, rather than waiting for it to
      expire — which is the behaviour a one-port range depends on, and which is why a session's video
      task stops the moment it is superseded.
      
      #### Firewall
      
      Open exactly the ports in use and nothing else:
      
      ```sh
      # shape A
      ufw allow 8443/tcp && ufw allow 9443/tcp && ufw allow 40000:40100/udp
      # shape B
      ufw allow 443/tcp  && ufw allow 9443/tcp && ufw allow 40000:40100/udp
      ```
      
      The video rule can only be written once `PEERINGD_VIDEO_PORTS` is set.
      
      #### Unit, and updating
      
      ```ini
      [Unit]
      Description=Peering relay
      After=network-online.target
      
      [Service]
      ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/peeringd
      //! The signalling conversation, as JSON over a WebSocket.
      //!
      //! This is the only place the two ends and the relay have to agree on a shape, and it is
      //! deliberately the smallest part of the system. Signalling carries no media — it introduces two
      //! parties and hands out the endpoints they will actually use. Once a session exists, nothing the
      //! relay says can affect what the two ends do with it, because every byte that matters is already
      //! authenticated between them.
      //!
      //! Field names are camelCase because the other end is Swift, where `JSONEncoder`'s default is the
      //! property name unchanged.
      
      use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
      
      use crate::session::Token;
      
      /// What a client — either a Mac or a phone — sends to the relay.
      #[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize, Serialize, PartialEq, Eq)]
      #[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "camelCase", rename_all_fields = "camelCase")]
      pub enum ClientMessage {
          /// A Mac announcing itself. Holding this connection open *is* the Mac's presence: when it
          /// drops, the Mac is offline, and it re-registers when it comes back — on a new address, under
          /// the same device ID.
          RegisterHost {
              device_id: String,
              name: String,
              protocol_version: u16,
          },
      
          /// A phone asking where its Mac is.
          ///
          /// `client_id` is the phone's own device ID, which it already broadcasts in its Bonjour TXT
          /// record and which is not a secret. The relay wants it for one reason: to recognise a
          /// reconnecting phone and supersede its previous session rather than accumulate one per
          /// attempt. Nothing here is authorization — see `session.rs`.
          ConnectToHost {
              host_id: String,
              client_id: String,
              protocol_version: u16,
          },
      
          /// Keeps the signalling connection alive through idle NAT timeouts.
          Ping,
      }
      
      /// What the relay sends back.
      #[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize, Serialize, PartialEq, Eq)]
      #[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "camelCase", rename_all_fields = "camelCase")]
      pub enum ServerMessage {
          /// A host registration was accepted.
          Registered { session_ttl_seconds: u64 },
      
          /// A session is ready. Sent to the phone that asked and pushed to the Mac it asked for, with
          /// identical contents, because both need exactly the same four things: where to connect and
          /// what to present when they get there.
          ///
          /// The control token is single-use; the video token is reusable, because a NAT mapping can
          /// change mid-session and the binding has to be re-established. See `session.rs`.
          SessionReady {
              control_host: String,
              control_port: u16,
              video_host: String,
              video_port: u16,
              /// Hex.
              control_token: String,
              /// Hex.
              video_token: String,
          },
      
          /// The Mac is not registered. It is asleep, off, or has not been launched.
          HostOffline { device_id: String },
      
          Pong,
      
          Error { code: String, message: String },
      }
      
      impl ServerMessage {
          pub fn error(code: &str, message: impl Into<String>) -> Self {
              Self::Error {
                  code: code.to_string(),
                  message: message.into(),
              }
          }
      }
      
      /// Hex, because it needs no dependency, is trivially readable in a log, and these are 16 bytes that
      /// travel inside TLS.
      pub fn hex(bytes: &Token) -> String {
          use std::fmt::Write;
          bytes
              .iter()
              .fold(String::with_capacity(bytes.len() * 2), |mut out, b| {
                  let _ = write!(out, "{b:02x}");
                  out
              })
      }
      
      pub fn unhex(text: &str) -> Option<Token> {
          if text.len() != 32 {
              return None;
          }
          let mut out = [0u8; 16];
          for (i, byte) in out.iter_mut().enumerate() {
              *byte = u8::from_str_radix(text.get(i * 2..i * 2 + 2)?, 16).ok()?;
          }
          Some(out)
      }
      
      #[cfg(test)]
      mod tests {
          use super::*;
      
          #[test]
          fn a_host_registration_round_trips_through_camel_case() {
              let text = r#"{"type":"registerHost","deviceId":"abc","name":"Studio","protocolVersion":3}"#;
              let message: ClientMessage = serde_json::from_str(text).expect("should parse");
              assert_eq!(
                  message,
                  ClientMessage::RegisterHost {
                      device_id: "abc".into(),
                      name: "Studio".into(),
                      protocol_version: 3,
                  }
              );
          }
      
          #[test]
          fn a_connect_request_round_trips_through_camel_case() {
              let text =
                  r#"{"type":"connectToHost","hostId":"mac","clientId":"phone","protocolVersion":3}"#;
              let message: ClientMessage = serde_json::from_str(text).expect("should parse");
              assert_eq!(
                  message,
                  ClientMessage::ConnectToHost {
                      host_id: "mac".into(),
                      client_id: "phone".into(),
                      protocol_version: 3,
                  }
              );
          }
      
          #[test]
          fn session_ready_reports_its_endpoints_in_the_case_swift_expects() {
              let message = ServerMessage::SessionReady {
                  control_host: "relay.example".into(),
                  control_port: 9443,
                  video_host: "relay.example".into(),
                  video_port: 51234,
                  control_token: hex(&[0xab; 16]),
                  video_token: hex(&[0xcd; 16]),
              };
              let json = serde_json::to_string(&message).expect("should encode");
      
              for key in [
                  "controlHost",
                  "controlPort",
                  "videoHost",
                  "videoPort",
                  "controlToken",
                  "videoToken",
              ] {
                  assert!(json.contains(key), "missing {key} in {json}");
              }
          }
      
          /// The Swift side decodes these by name, so a rename here is a silent break at runtime rather
          /// than a compile error there. This pins the tag as well as the fields.
          #[test]
          fn the_message_tag_is_the_swift_case_name() {
              let json = serde_json::to_string(&ServerMessage::Pong).unwrap();
              assert_eq!(json, r#"{"type":"pong"}"#);
      
              let json = serde_json::to_string(&ServerMessage::HostOffline {
                  device_id: "abc".into(),
              })
              .unwrap();
              assert_eq!(json, r#"{"type":"hostOffline","deviceId":"abc"}"#);
          }
      
          #[test]
          fn tokens_survive_a_round_trip_and_rubbish_is_refused() {
              let token = [
                  0x01, 0x23, 0x45, 0x67, 0x89, 0xab, 0xcd, 0xef, 0xfe, 0xdc, 0xba, 0x98, 0x76, 0x54,
                  0x32, 0x10,
              ];
              assert_eq!(unhex(&hex(&token)), Some(token));
      
              assert_eq!(unhex(""), None);
              assert_eq!(unhex("abcd"), None, "too short");
              assert_eq!(unhex(&"z".repeat(32)), None, "not hex");
              assert_eq!(unhex(&"a".repeat(33)), None, "too long");
              assert_eq!(unhex(&"aB".repeat(16)), Some([0xab; 16]), "either case");
          }
      }
      //! The whole relay, exercised the way the two apps will use it.
      //!
      //! The unit tests check each piece against its own rules; this checks the pieces against each
      //! other, over real sockets. Everything below is what `RelayClient.swift` and `HostServer.swift`
      //! will have to do: register, ask, receive a session, present a token on a control socket, and
      //! bind a video address — so a mistake in the *shape* of the protocol shows up here rather than on
      //! a phone in another country.
      
      use std::net::SocketAddr;
      use std::sync::Arc;
      use std::time::Duration;
      
      use futures_util::{SinkExt, StreamExt};
      use tokio::io::{AsyncReadExt, AsyncWriteExt};
      use tokio::net::{TcpListener, TcpStream, UdpSocket};
      use tokio::time::timeout;
      use tokio_tungstenite::tungstenite::Message;
      
      use peeringd::protocol::{unhex, ClientMessage, ServerMessage};
      use peeringd::session::Registry;
      use peeringd::signalling::{HostRegistry, Settings};
      use peeringd::udp_relay::{bind_packet, PortPool};
      use peeringd::{signalling, tcp_relay};
      
      /// Generous enough to absorb a loaded CI machine, short enough that a hang fails the test rather
      /// than the suite.
      const PATIENCE: Duration = Duration::from_secs(5);
      
      type Ws = tokio_tungstenite::WebSocketStream<tokio_tungstenite::MaybeTlsStream<TcpStream>>;
      
      struct TestRelay {
          signal_port: u16,
          control_port: u16,
      }
      
      /// The endpoints a session hands to one end.
      struct Session {
          control_token: String,
          video_port: u16,
          video_token: String,
      }
      
      async fn start() -> TestRelay {
          let registry = Arc::new(Registry::new());
      
          // Port 0 throughout, so tests never collide with a relay someone is actually running — or with
          // each other when the suite runs them in parallel.
          let control = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0").await.unwrap();
          let control_port = control.local_addr().unwrap().port();
          let signal = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0").await.unwrap();
          let signal_port = signal.local_addr().unwrap().port();
      
          tokio::spawn(tcp_relay::serve(control, Arc::clone(&registry)));
      
          tokio::spawn(signalling::serve(
              signal,
              registry,
              HostRegistry::new(),
              Settings {
                  host: Some("127.0.0.1".into()),
                  public_control_port: control_port,
                  video_bind: "127.0.0.1:0".parse().unwrap(),
                  video_ports: Arc::new(PortPool::new(None)),
                  public_video_port: None,
                  session_ttl: Duration::from_secs(60),
              },
              None,
          ));
      
          TestRelay {
              signal_port,
              control_port,
          }
      }
      
      async fn connect(port: u16) -> Ws {
          let (ws, _) = timeout(
              PATIENCE,
              tokio_tungstenite::connect_async(format!("ws://127.0.0.1:{port}")),
          )
          .await
          .expect("the signalling socket should open")
          .expect("the websocket handshake should succeed");
          ws
      }
      
      async fn send(ws: &mut Ws, message: &ClientMessage) {
          let json = serde_json::to_string(message).unwrap();
          ws.send(Message::Text(json.into())).await.unwrap();
      }
      
      /// The next message from the relay, whatever it is.
      async fn next_message(ws: &mut Ws) -> ServerMessage {
          loop {
              let message = timeout(PATIENCE, ws.next())
                  .await
                  .expect("timed out waiting for a message")
                  .expect("the stream ended early")
                  .expect("the websocket errored");
      
              if let Message::Text(text) = message {
                  return serde_json::from_str(&text).expect("should parse as ServerMessage");
              }
          }
      }
      
      /// Reads until a `SessionReady` arrives, skipping the traffic that can legitimately precede one.
      async fn await_session(ws: &mut Ws) -> Session {
          loop {
              match next_message(ws).await {
                  ServerMessage::SessionReady {
                      control_token,
                      video_port,
                      video_token,
                      ..
                  } => {
                      return Session {
                          control_token,
                          video_port,
                          video_token,
                      }
                  }
                  ServerMessage::Registered { .. } | ServerMessage::Pong => continue,
                  other => panic!("expected a session, got {other:?}"),
              }
          }
      }
      
      /// Opens a control socket and presents the token, exactly as the apps will: the token first, in
      /// the clear, and whatever follows it belongs to somebody else.
      async fn present(control_port: u16, token: &str) -> TcpStream {
          let mut stream = TcpStream::connect(("127.0.0.1", control_port))
              .await
              .expect("the control relay should accept");
          stream
              .write_all(&unhex(token).expect("the token should be hex"))
              .await
              .unwrap();
          stream
      }
      
      /// Registers a Mac and waits for the registration to be acknowledged.
      ///
      /// Waiting rather than firing and forgetting is what stops the acknowledgement sitting in the
      /// stream to be tripped over by whichever read comes next.
      async fn register_mac(relay: &TestRelay, device_id: &str) -> Ws {
          let mut mac = connect(relay.signal_port).await;
          send(
              &mut mac,
              &ClientMessage::RegisterHost {
                  device_id: device_id.into(),
                  name: "Studio".into(),
                  protocol_version: 3,
              },
          )
          .await;
      
          assert!(
              matches!(next_message(&mut mac).await, ServerMessage::Registered { .. }),
              "the relay should acknowledge a registration"
          );
      
          mac
      }
      
      #[tokio::test]
      async fn a_mac_and_a_phone_are_introduced_and_their_control_sockets_talk() {
          let relay = start().await;
          let mut mac = register_mac(&relay, "mac").await;
      
          let mut phone = connect(relay.signal_port).await;
          send(
              &mut phone,
              &ClientMessage::ConnectToHost {
                  host_id: "mac".into(),
                  client_id: "phone".into(),
                  protocol_version: 3,
              },
          )
          .await;
      
          let phone_session = await_session(&mut phone).await;
          let mac_session = await_session(&mut mac).await;
      
          // Both ends present the same control token. Whichever arrives first waits for the other, and
          // whoever is holding both splices — so neither of these calls returns a usable stream until
          // the second one has been made.
          let mut phone_side = present(relay.control_port, &phone_session.control_token).await;
          let mut mac_side = present(relay.control_port, &mac_session.control_token).await;
      
          phone_side.write_all(b"a click").await.unwrap();
      
          let mut heard = [0u8; 7];
          timeout(PATIENCE, mac_side.read_exact(&mut heard))
              .await
              .expect("the Mac should hear the phone")
              .unwrap();
          assert_eq!(&heard, b"a click");
      
          // And back the other way, which is what proves the splice is bidirectional rather than a pair
          // of one-way pipes that happen to have been wired the same way round.
          mac_side.write_all(b"a frame").await.unwrap();
      
          let mut back = [0u8; 7];
          timeout(PATIENCE, phone_side.read_exact(&mut back))
              .await
              .expect("the phone should hear the Mac")
              .unwrap();
          assert_eq!(&back, b"a frame");
      }

          let mut mac = register_mac(&relay, "mac").await;
      
          let mut phone = connect(relay.signal_port).await;
          send(
              &mut phone,

      # MacCast — macOS host + iOS client remote desktop
      
      ## Context
      
      MacCast is a greenfield build of the architecture spec: a macOS **host** that captures its
      screen and injects synthetic input, driven by an iOS **client** over local Wi-Fi, with a
      persistent device identity so the Mac is recognised across networks.
      
      The repo currently holds an **untouched iOS SwiftUI+SwiftData template** (`a944be4 Initial
      Commit`). Nothing in the spec exists yet. A concrete surprise worth stating up front: despite
      the name `MacCast`, the existing target is an **iOS app**, not macOS — `SDKROOT = iphoneos`,
      `TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY = "1,2"`, and `ContentView.swift` uses iOS-only APIs
      (`.navigationBarTrailing`, `EditButton()`). There is no `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET` in the project.
      
      **Confirmed decisions:** keep the iOS target as the client and add a macOS host target to the
      same project, with shared code in a local `RemoteCore` package; build the full vertical slice
      including live streaming; encrypt the channel over TLS with a runtime-generated self-signed
      identity and authenticate pairing via a 6-digit SAS comparison; the iOS keyboard supports **both**
      Unicode and keycode modes with a toggle; the client can **switch capture sources** mid-session —
      display, whole application, or single window — behind a `CaptureSource` abstraction; unit tests
      focus on `RemoteCore`.
      
      **Environment:** Xcode 26.6, Swift 6.3.3, iOS/macOS 26.5 SDKs, macOS 26.6.2 arm64. An iPhone 15
      Pro Max is paired and valid signing identities exist — end-to-end testing is possible on real
      hardware, which matters because Bonjour and local-network permission are unreliable in the
      Simulator.
      
      ---
      
      ## Verified defects in the spec's sample code
      
      Checked against the on-disk SDKs and the compiler, not assumed. The sample code is illustrative,
      but several of these are load-bearing enough to change the design.
      
      **1. `RemoteCommand` cannot compile on iOS — defeating the point of sharing it.** The spec
      presents it as the shared cross-platform model, but it uses two macOS-only types:
      
      | Type used | Why it fails on iOS |
      |---|---|
      | `NSEvent.ModifierFlags.RawValue` | `AppKit.framework` is **absent from the iOS SDK** (verified) |
      | `CGKeyCode` | Defined in `CGRemoteOperation.h`, **absent from the iOS SDK** (verified) |
      
      Fix: `RemoteCore` speaks platform-neutral primitives — `UInt16` keycode, `UInt` modifiers,
      `Double` coordinates. The macOS side translates to `CGKeyCode`/`CGEventFlags` at the injection
      boundary and nowhere else.
      
      **2. The modifier bit values are correct but should still be replaced.** Verified against
      `NSEvent.h`: shift `1<<17`, control `1<<18`, option `1<<19`, command `1<<20` — they line up with
      `kCGEventFlagMask*`. So the spec's hardcoded numbers (131072/262144/524288/1048576) do work, but
      they are an AppKit bit layout living inside a shared module. Define a real `OptionSet` in
      `RemoteCore`.
      
      **3. Three `CGEvent` calls do not compile.** Verified with `swiftc`: `CGEvent(mouseEventSource:
      nil)` is rejected — *incorrect argument label in call (have 'mouseEventSource:', expected
      'source:')*. Appears in `mouseDown`, `mouseUp`, `joystickMove`.
      
      **4. `processIncomingData(_ data: CGSize)`** is declared `CGSize` but called with `Data`.
      
      **5. No message framing — the most important correctness bug.**
      `receive(minimumIncompleteLength: 4, maximumLength: 65536)` returns an arbitrary byte window.
      JSON-over-TCP has no message boundaries, so back-to-back commands arrive fused (decode failure)
      and large ones arrive split (decode failure). The `4` hints at a length prefix never implemented.
      **Every command depends on this**, so framing is built first.
      
      **6. `activeConnection` is never cleared** on error/`isComplete`, leaking the old connection.
      And `if !isComplete && error == nil { receiveLoop }` silently drops remainders.
      
      **7. `switchSpace` is correct** — Ctrl+←/→ (`123`/`124`) is the real Spaces shortcut. Keep it.
      
      ---
      
      ## Target layout
      
      ```
      MacCast.xcodeproj
      ├── MacCast        (iOS app)     ← existing, becomes the client
      ├── MacCastHost    (macOS app)   ← NEW
      ├── RemoteCore     (local SPM)   ← NEW: framing, protocol, crypto, coordinate mapping
      ├── MacCastTests
      └── MacCastUITests
      ```
      
      The project uses `PBXFileSystemSynchronizedRootGroup` (objectVersion 77), so new `.swift` files
      under a synced folder need **zero pbxproj edits**. Adding the macOS target and the package
      reference does require pbxproj edits — mechanical, and verified immediately with
      `xcodebuild -list` plus a real build. Do **not** hand-write file entries into build phases; let
      the sync groups do it. Keep the existing `MacCast` iOS target's `SWIFT_DEFAULT_ACTOR_ISOLATION =
      MainActor` (it suits UI), but give the **macOS host target** nonisolated default — capture,
      encode, and networking code must not be MainActor-bound.
      
      ---
      
      ## Wire protocol (`RemoteCore`)
      
      ### Framing — built first
      
      ```
      ┌──────────────┬─────────┬─────────────────────┐
      │ u32 length   │ u8 kind │ payload (length-1)  │
      │ big-endian   │         │                     │
      └──────────────┴─────────┴─────────────────────┘
      ```
      
      A `FrameDecoder` accumulates bytes and emits whole frames, handling partial and coalesced reads.
      **Enforce a hard length cap (16 MiB) before allocating** — otherwise a corrupt or hostile length
      field is an instant memory-exhaustion DoS on the host.
      
      ### Two connections, not one
      
      The client opens **control** and **video** connections. Sharing one TCP stream causes
      head-of-line blocking: a 200 KB keyframe sits in front of the next mouse move, adding ~50 ms of
      jitter at 30 Mbps. Control latency is what a user feels; it must never queue behind video. One
      `NWListener` on port 51515 accepts both; the first frame declares the role.
      
      ### Handshake and pairing
      
      Unauthenticated phase, then everything is sealed:
      
      1. `C→S clientHello` — `{ clientId, protoVersion, wantsPairing }`
      2. `S→C serverHello` — `{ serverId, hostName, serverIdentityPub, alreadyPaired }`
      3. **TLS handshake** runs here, with the client pinning the server's SPKI. From this point the
         channel is encrypted and forward-secret; app-layer messages need no separate envelope.
      4. **Unpaired (SAS):** both sides derive 6 digits from the handshake transcript — both ephemeral
         public keys plus `serverIdentityPub` — and display them. The user compares and confirms. On
         match the client stores `{serverId, serverIdentityPub}` in the **Keychain** and pins it.
      5. **Paired:** the client verifies the pinned `serverIdentityPub`. No user interaction.
         Client→host authentication is mTLS via `sec_protocol_options_set_challenge_block`.
      
      The transcript must be hashed **in a fixed, agreed order** and cover every field the peers
      exchanged, or the comparison is meaningless. Comparisons are **constant-time** — Swift's `Data ==`
      short-circuits, so use a `timingsafe_bcmp`-style loop. Both of these are pinned by unit tests.
      
      ### Transport security: TLS with a runtime-generated identity
      
      **A correction to an earlier draft of this plan.** I first concluded that TLS-PSK was a dead end
      because `tls_ciphersuite_t` declares no PSK suites. That was **too strong and is retracted**:
      `tls_ciphersuite_t` is a `CF_ENUM(uint16_t, ...)`, so a PSK suite can be constructed from a raw
      value, and Apple's own sample does exactly that. The enum not *declaring* them does not make them
      unreachable.
      
      The real case against TLS-PSK is stronger than the one I made, and it is about security rather
      than reachability:
      
      - **It is TLS 1.2-only.** Both min *and* max must be pinned to `.TLSv1_2`, because
        Network.framework offers TLS 1.3 first.
      - **`TLS_PSK_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256` is plain PSK — no (EC)DHE, so no forward secrecy.** Every key
        derives from the PSK plus public randoms, which means **a passive eavesdropper who records one
        handshake can brute-force a 6-digit PIN offline.** 10⁶ HMACs is instant. That alone disqualifies
        it for a PIN-based pairing scheme.
      - There is a documented history of platform regressions (`PSK_IDENTITY NOT FOUND`), and Apple's own
        TicTacToe sample drew a filed security bug over a 4-digit PIN without an endorsed fix.
      
      **So: TLS 1.3 with a self-signed identity minted on the host and pinned by the client.** This is
      also closer to your original choice than the CryptoKit fallback I floated, and it keeps the record
      layer, forward secrecy, replay protection and rekeying in a stack Apple maintains and
      hardware-accelerates. Self-signed is not weaker than CA-signed *provided the client pins* — if
      anything stronger, since there is no CA to coerce.
      
      The path, all documented APIs:
      
      ```
      SecKeyCreateRandomKey(P-256, kSecAttrIsPermanent: true)   // keychain-backed on purpose
        → X509.Certificate(self-signed)  via apple/swift-certificates
        → SecCertificateCreateWithData(der)
        → SecIdentityCreate(cert, key)        // iOS 11.2+ / macOS 10.12+, not deprecated
        → sec_identity_create → sec_protocol_options_set_local_identity
      ```
      
      Client side pins the server's **SPKI** (not leaf bytes, so the cert can rotate without re-pairing)
      via `sec_protocol_options_set_verify_block` → `sec_trust_copy_ref` →
      `SecTrustCopyCertificateChain` → `Certificates[0]` → `SecKeyCopyExternalRepresentation`.
      
      Two risks, both bounded:
      1. **`SecIdentityCreate` may require a keychain-backed key** — widely claimed, not verifiable from
         Apple docs. Mitigated by `kSecAttrIsPermanent: true`, with a documented fallback to
         `SecItemImport` (not `SecItemAdd`, which skips populating the public-key hash). **This is a
         ~30-minute spike in Phase 0 that gates the whole crypto design — do it before building on it.**
      2. It adds a dependency tree — `apple/swift-certificates` (verified: release 1.20.0, actively
         maintained, not archived, `swift-tools-version:6.1`, and **no `platforms:` constraint** so it
         builds for these targets), which in turn brings `apple/swift-crypto` and `apple/swift-asn1`.
         All three are Apple-maintained. `swift-certificates` is the only supported way to build X.509
         DER on-device without hand-rolling it.
      
      **Fallback if the spike fails:** `swift-noise` (validated against the official Noise test vectors)
      for a real `XXpsk2` handshake. Do **not** hand-roll a record layer from CryptoKit primitives — the
      rekey/replay/nonce state machine is exactly where hand-rolled crypto goes wrong, and it is not
      worth owning for this.
      
      ### Pairing must change to numeric comparison (SAS)
      
      **The PIN scheme as specified in the draft was cryptographically unsound, and this is a real
      correction rather than a refinement.** A 6-digit PIN used as a client→host proof is
      **offline-brute-forceable by an active attacker during first pairing**: the attacker substitutes
      their own identity, receives the PIN-derived MAC over *their* transcript, and then tries all 10⁶
      candidates instantly. Rate limiting does not help, because the guess happens off-line.
      
      **Fix: SAS / numeric comparison — the Bluetooth LE model.** After the encrypted channel is up, both
      sides independently derive 6 digits from the handshake transcript (both ephemeral public keys plus
      the server's long-term public key) and the user confirms the two screens match. An active
      man-in-the-middle now succeeds with probability 10⁻⁶ *per attempt*, and it cannot grind offline.
      
      UX cost is small — the Mac still shows 6 digits; the iOS client shows its own and the user taps
      "Match" instead of typing. Security gain is the difference between a broken scheme and a sound one.
      After pairing, the host's long-term identity key is pinned in the iOS Keychain with
      `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly`, and later connections need no user interaction.
      
      Post-pairing client→host authentication uses **mTLS** (`sec_protocol_options_set_challenge_block`)
      rather than an app-layer bearer token — a tool that can drive someone's Mac warrants mutual auth.
      
      ### Commands (sealed)
      
      Platform-neutral types throughout — the fix for defect #1:
      
      ```
      mouseMove(x: Double, y: Double)          // NORMALIZED 0…1
      mouseDown(button: UInt8) / mouseUp(button: UInt8)
      scroll(dx: Double, dy: Double)
      keyDown(keyCode: UInt16, modifiers: UInt) / keyUp(...)
      switchSpace(direction: .left | .right)
      joystickMove(dx: Double, dy: Double)
      textInput(String)                        // Unicode mode
      setCaptureSource(CaptureSource)          // client-driven source switch
      ```
      
      **Both keyboard paths are implemented, with a client-side toggle.** They are genuinely different
      mechanisms, not two spellings of one:
      
      - **Unicode mode** — `textInput` → host injects via `CGEventKeyboardSetUnicodeString`. Layout-
        independent, so emoji, CJK and accented characters all work. Weakness: some app shortcuts that
        listen for physical keycodes will not fire.
      - **Keycode mode** — `keyDown`/`keyUp` with real keycodes and modifiers. `Cmd+S`, `Cmd+Tab` and
        games behave exactly as a physical keyboard. Weakness: output depends on the Mac's active layout.
      
      `switchSpace` and the modifier toggles belong to keycode mode and compose with it naturally.
      
      ### Capture sources — the abstraction
      
      Per-app viewing is a first-class use case (switch between apps, not just displays), so the source
      is modelled as a type from the start rather than as a display ID that later grows a second meaning:
      
      ```swift
      public enum CaptureSource: Codable, Sendable, Hashable {
          case display(UInt32)       // CGDirectDisplayID  raw value
          case application(Int32)    // pid_t — all of that app's windows, composited
          case window(UInt32)        // CGWindowID raw value
      }
      ```
      
      **Platform-neutral raw values on purpose** — `CGDirectDisplayID` and `CGWindowID` live in
      macOS-only headers, so using them directly would repeat defect #1 and break the iOS build.
      
      The host enumerates what is available and pushes a *catalog* to the client, which renders it as a
      picker. This is what makes the feature discoverable rather than a hardcoded list:
      
      ```swift
      public struct CaptureSourceDescriptor: Codable, Sendable, Identifiable, Hashable {
          public enum Kind: String, Codable, Sendable { case display, application, window }
          public let id: UUID            // stable identity for the client's list
          public let kind: Kind
          public let title: String       // "Built-in Display" · "Xcode" · "ContentView.swift"

      description: Test-driven development. Use when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions "red-green-refactor", or wants integration tests.
      ---
      
      # Test-Driven Development
      
      TDD is the red → green loop. This skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle: consult them before and during the loop, not after.
      
      When exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.
      
      ## What a good test is
      
      Tests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely; tests shouldn't. A good test reads like a specification: "user can checkout with valid cart" tells you exactly what capability exists, and it survives refactors because it doesn't care about internal structure.
      
      See [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for mocking guidelines.
      
      ## Seams: where tests go
      
      A **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.
      
      **Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything, so agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.
      
      Ask: "What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?"
      
      When the shape of that interface is itself in question (how deep the module is, where the seam belongs, what the interface should expose), call the Skill tool with "codebase-design" for the vocabulary. It is the shared source of the module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage and locality terms, and it is a reference to consult, not a session to run.
      
      ## Anti-patterns
      
      - **Implementation-coupled**: mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (querying the database instead of using the interface). The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed.
      - **Tautological**: the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does (`expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`, a snapshot derived by hand the same way, a constant asserted equal to itself), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code. Expected values must come from an independent source of truth: a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.
      - **Horizontal slicing**: writing all tests first, then all implementation. Bulk tests verify _imagined_ behavior: you test the _shape_ of things rather than user-facing behavior, the tests go insensitive to real changes, and you commit to test structure before understanding the implementation. Work in **vertical slices** instead: one test → one implementation → repeat, each test a **tracer bullet** that responds to what the last cycle taught you.
      
      ## Rules of the loop
      
      - **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.
      - **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.
      - **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.

      # MacCast domain glossary
      
      ## Capture source
      
      Something the host can stream now: a display, a running application, or a window.
      
      ## Running application
      
      A user-facing application process that currently owns capturable content. It has a process
      identity and can therefore be selected as a capture source.
      
      ## Installed application
      
      A user-facing application available on the host but not currently running. It can be launched,
      but it is not a capture source until it becomes a running application.
      
      ## Application catalogue
      
      The host's current, user-facing list of running and installed applications. Background agents,
      menu extras, helper processes, and duplicate instances are not applications in this catalogue.
      // swift-tools-version: 6.1

      // RemoteCore is shared by the macOS host and the iOS client, so it may only use
      // frameworks present on both: Foundation, Crypto, Security, Network and CoreGraphics.
      // Anything macOS-only (ScreenCaptureKit, VideoToolbox, AppKit) belongs in the host
      // target — this module is compiled for iOS too, where those frameworks do not exist.
      //
      // swift-certificates is the one external dependency, and it is shared rather than
      // host-only because both sides mint a self-signed identity and pin the peer's SPKI.
      let package = Package(
          name: "RemoteCore",
          platforms: [.iOS(.v17), .macOS(.v14)],
          products: [
              .library(name: "RemoteCore", targets: ["RemoteCore"]),

          dependencies: [
              .package(url: "https://github.com/apple/swift-certificates.git", from: "1.20.0"),

                  dependencies: [
                      .product(name: "X509", package: "swift-certificates"),
                      .product(name: "SwiftASN1", package: "swift-asn1"),
                  ],
                  swiftSettings: [.swiftLanguageMode(.v6)]
              ),
              .testTarget(
                  name: "RemoteCoreTests",
                  dependencies: ["RemoteCore"],
                  swiftSettings: [.swiftLanguageMode(.v6)]
              ),
          ]
      )
      import Foundation
      import Network
      import RemoteCore
      import os
      
      private let videoLog = Logger(subsystem: "pl.dmq.peering.host", category: "video")
      
      /// Advertises the host over Bonjour and accepts both connection roles.
      ///
      /// One listener serves the control and video channels; the first frame on each connection
      /// declares which it is. They are separate TCP connections on purpose — sharing one stream
      /// would put a 200 KB keyframe in front of the next mouse move, and control latency is
      /// exactly what a user feels.
      ///
      /// All mutable state is confined to ``queue``. Everything crossing out of it does so as a
      /// ``HostEvent``.
      final class HostServer: @unchecked Sendable {
          private let queue = DispatchQueue(label: "pl.dmq.peering.host.server")
      
          private let identity: SelfSignedIdentity
          private let device: DeviceIdentity
          private let pins: PinStore
      
          private var listener: NWListener?
          private var controlSessions: [HostSession] = []
      
          /// Each video connection is tagged with the client key that authorized it, so it can be
          /// torn down when that client's control session ends.
          private var videoConnections: [(peer: PeerConnection, clientKey: Data)] = []
      
          private let callbackLock = NSLock()
          private var _onEvent: (@Sendable (HostEvent) -> Void)?
          private var _onCommand: (@Sendable (RemoteCommand) -> Void)?
          private var _onVideoConnection: (@Sendable (PeerConnection) -> Void)?
      
          var onEvent: (@Sendable (HostEvent) -> Void)? {
              get { callbackLock.withLock { _onEvent } }
              set { callbackLock.withLock { _onEvent = newValue } }
          }
      
          var onCommand: (@Sendable (RemoteCommand) -> Void)? {
              get { callbackLock.withLock { _onCommand } }
              set { callbackLock.withLock { _onCommand = newValue } }
          }
      
          var onVideoConnection: (@Sendable (PeerConnection) -> Void)? {
              get { callbackLock.withLock { _onVideoConnection } }
              set { callbackLock.withLock { _onVideoConnection = newValue } }
          }
      
          enum Failure: LocalizedError {
              case invalidPort(UInt16)
              case listenerFailed(String)
      
              var errorDescription: String? {
                  switch self {
                  case .invalidPort(let port):
                      return "Port \(port) is not a usable TCP port."
                  case .listenerFailed(let reason):
                      return "The listener could not start: \(reason)"
                  }
              }
          }
      
          init(identity: SelfSignedIdentity, device: DeviceIdentity, pins: PinStore) {
              self.identity = identity
              self.device = device
              self.pins = pins
          }
      
          // The bound port is reported through `.listening(port:)` rather than stored here.
          // Writing it on the queue and reading it from the UI would be a data race for no gain.
      
          // MARK: - Lifecycle
      
          func start() throws {
              guard listener == nil else { return }
      
              let tls = try TLSConfig.serverOptions(identity: identity, queue: queue)
              let tcp = NWProtocolTCP.Options()
              tcp.noDelay = true
              let parameters = NWParameters(tls: tls, tcp: tcp)
              // Without this a restart during development fails to bind for up to a minute.
              parameters.allowLocalEndpointReuse = true
      
              guard let port = NWEndpoint.Port(rawValue: ProtocolInfo.defaultPort) else {
                  throw Failure.invalidPort(ProtocolInfo.defaultPort)
              }
      
              let listener: NWListener
              do {
                  listener = try NWListener(using: parameters, on: port)
              } catch {
                  throw Failure.listenerFailed(error.localizedDescription)
              }
      
              // The TXT record carries the persistent device ID, which is what lets a client
              // recognise this Mac across networks and DHCP leases. The ID is stable; the
              // advertised address is not.
              let txt = NWTXTRecord([
                  ProtocolInfo.TXTRecordKey.deviceID: device.id,
                  ProtocolInfo.TXTRecordKey.deviceName: device.name,
                  ProtocolInfo.TXTRecordKey.protocolVersion: String(ProtocolInfo.version),
              ])
              listener.service = NWListener.Service(
                  name: device.name,
                  type: ProtocolInfo.bonjourServiceType,
                  txtRecord: txt
              )
      
              listener.stateUpdateHandler = { [weak self] state in
                  guard let self else { return }
                  switch state {
                  case .ready:
                      emit(.listening(port: listener.port?.rawValue ?? ProtocolInfo.defaultPort))
                  case .failed(let error):
                      emit(.failed(error.localizedDescription))
                      stop()
                  case .cancelled:
                      emit(.stopped)
                  default:
                      break
                  }
              }
      
              listener.newConnectionHandler = { [weak self] connection in
                  self?.accept(connection)
              }
      
              self.listener = listener
              listener.start(queue: queue)
          }
      
          func stop() {
              // Strong capture: HostModel sets server = nil immediately after calling stop(), which
              // can deallocate the server before the async block runs. A weak capture would then
              // skip listener?.cancel(), leaving the port held and the next start() unable to bind.
              queue.async { [self] in
                  listener?.cancel()
                  listener = nil
                  for session in controlSessions { session.cancel() }
                  for entry in videoConnections { entry.peer.cancel() }
                  controlSessions.removeAll()
                  videoConnections.removeAll()
              }
          }
      
          /// Forgets every paired client. The UI calls this after confirming with the user.
          func unpairAll() -> Bool {
              pins.removeAll()
          }
      
          var pairedClientIDs: [String] { pins.peerIDs }
      
          // MARK: - Connections
      
          private func accept(_ connection: NWConnection) {
              let peer = PeerConnection(connection: connection, queue: queue)
      
              let session = HostSession(
                  connection: peer,
                  identity: identity,
                  device: device,
                  pins: pins,
                  emit: { [weak self] event in self?.emit(event) }
              )
              session.onCommand = { [weak self] command in
                  self?.onCommand?(command)
              }
              session.onVideoConnection = { [weak self] videoPeer in
                  guard let self else { return }
                  guard let key = videoPeer.peerPublicKey,
                        controlSessions.contains(where: { $0.isAuthorized && $0.peerPublicKey == key })
                  else {
                      // **This is the only thing authorizing a video connection, so it is not a
                      // formality.** A video connection carries no handshake of its own — it does
                      // not even say which client it belongs to — and the server's TLS verify
                      // block deliberately accepts any self-signed chain, because authenticity in
                      // this design comes from pairing rather than from a CA. So "completed a TLS
                      // handshake" proves nothing at all, and without this check any peer that can
                      // reach the port could ask for the user's screen and get it.
                      //
                      // The client key is the thing that ties the two sockets together: it comes
                      // from the peer's certificate, so a client cannot claim one it does not hold.
                      videoLog.notice("refused a video connection with no authorized control session")
                      emit(.failed("Refused a video connection from an unauthorized client"))
                      videoPeer.cancel()
                      return
                  }
      
                  videoConnections.append((peer: videoPeer, clientKey: key))
                  onVideoConnection?(videoPeer)
              }
      
              session.onEnded = { [weak self] in
                  guard let self else { return }
                  // Pruning matters for more than tidiness — a finished session left in the list
                  // would go on authorizing video connections, since `isAuthorized` stays true on
                  // an object whose connection is gone.
                  controlSessions.removeAll { $0 === session }
                  // And the streams authorized by it end with it. "Stop sharing" has to actually
                  // stop: a video connection that outlived its control session would keep
                  // delivering the screen to a client the host believes is gone.
                  closeVideoConnections(for: session.peerPublicKey)
              }
      
              controlSessions.append(session)
              session.start()
          }
      
          /// Pushes an updated capture catalogue to every authorized client.
          ///
          /// Every client, not the one that caused the change: the catalogue is host-wide state,
          /// and two devices looking at the same Mac disagreeing about what is capturable is a
          /// bug the user would see as one of them offering a source that no longer exists.
          ///
          /// Hops to the server queue because that is where `controlSessions` lives and where
          /// every session mutates its state — see ``HostSession``.
          func broadcastCatalog(_ catalog: CaptureCatalog) {
              queue.async { [weak self] in
                  guard let self else { return }
                  for session in self.controlSessions {
                      session.sendCatalog(catalog)
                  }
              }
          }
      
          private func closeVideoConnections(for clientKey: Data?) {
              guard let clientKey else { return }
              let closing = videoConnections.filter { $0.clientKey == clientKey }
              videoConnections.removeAll { $0.clientKey == clientKey }
              for entry in closing { entry.peer.cancel() }
          }
      
          private func emit(_ event: HostEvent) {
              onEvent?(event)
          }
      }
