      private let modelLog = Logger(subsystem: "pl.dmq.peering", category: "app")
      
      /// Which keyboard the user is driving the Mac with.
      ///
      /// The two modes are not a preference, they are different protocols on the wire, and the
      /// difference is user-visible:
      ///
      /// - ``unicode`` sends ``RemoteCommand/textInput(_:)``, which the host injects as Unicode
      ///   text. Layout-independent, so emoji, accented characters and CJK all arrive intact —
      ///   but a Mac shortcut that listens for a *physical* keycode (⌘S, ⌘Tab) never fires,
      ///   because no key was ever pressed.
      /// - ``keycode`` sends ``RemoteCommand/keyDown(keyCode:modifiers:)`` and ``keyUp`` with real
      ///   macOS virtual keycodes, so shortcuts behave exactly as they do on a hardware keyboard.
      ///   The cost is that a character with no keycode on the Mac's layout cannot be expressed.
      enum KeyboardMode: String, CaseIterable, Identifiable {
          case unicode
          case keycode
      
          var id: String { rawValue }
      
          var label: String {
              switch self {
              case .unicode: return "Unicode"
              case .keycode: return "Keycode"
              }
          }
      
          var explanation: String {
              switch self {
              case .unicode:
                  return "Sends text. Emoji and non-Latin scripts work; Mac shortcuts like ⌘S do not."
              case .keycode:
                  return "Sends real key presses with modifiers. Shortcuts work; characters outside the Mac's layout cannot be typed."
              }
          }
      }
      
      /// One macro button: a keycode with modifiers, sent as a press and a release.
      struct Macro: Identifiable, Hashable {
          let id: String
          let title: String
          let keyCode: UInt16
          let modifiers: Modifiers
      
          static let defaults: [Macro] = [
              // Keycodes are macOS virtual keycodes — the values `CGEvent` takes — not USB HID
              // usages and not characters. C is 8, V is 9, W is 13, Tab is 48, Space is 49.
              Macro(id: "copy", title: "⌘C", keyCode: 8, modifiers: .command),
              Macro(id: "paste", title: "⌘V", keyCode: 9, modifiers: .command),
              Macro(id: "cut", title: "⌘X", keyCode: 7, modifiers: .command),
              Macro(id: "undo", title: "⌘Z", keyCode: 6, modifiers: .command),
              Macro(id: "save", title: "⌘S", keyCode: 1, modifiers: .command),
              Macro(id: "close", title: "⌘W", keyCode: 13, modifiers: .command),
              Macro(id: "appswitch", title: "⌘⇥", keyCode: 48, modifiers: .command),
              Macro(id: "spotlight", title: "⌘Space", keyCode: 49, modifiers: .command),
              Macro(id: "escape", title: "esc", keyCode: 53, modifiers: []),
              Macro(id: "return", title: "⏎", keyCode: 36, modifiers: []),
          ]
      }
      
      /// Everything the UI binds to.
      ///
      /// One owner of the session, the identity and the renderer, so there is exactly one place
      /// where a network event becomes observable state — and exactly one place to look when the
      /// screen shows something that does not match what the Mac is doing.
      @Observable
      @MainActor
      final class SessionModel {
          // MARK: - Connection state
      
          private(set) var phase: ClientSession.Phase = .idle
          private(set) var hosts: [DiscoveredHost] = []
          private(set) var browseStatus = "Looking for Macs on this network…"
          private(set) var hostName: String?
          private(set) var tlsDescription: String?
          private(set) var latencyMilliseconds: Double?
          private(set) var catalog: CaptureCatalog?
          private(set) var notes: [String] = []
          private(set) var videoStatus = "No video stream"
          private(set) var pairedHostIDs: [String] = []
      
          /// What each trusted Mac is called, by the ID its pin is keyed by.
          ///
          /// The pin store knows only the ID, so the picker was listing `A1B2C3…` where the user
          /// expects the name of their Mac. The handshake is the only moment the client is told both,
          /// so it is the only moment this can be recorded.
          private(set) var hostNames: [String: String] = [:]
      
          private static let hostNamesKey = "Peering.hostNames"
      
          /// The failure to show the user, if the session is in one.
          ///
          /// The phase carries it and the diagnostics screen has always listed it, but the picker
          /// showed nothing at all — so a connection that failed instantly looked exactly like a
          /// button that did not work, which is a worse failure than the one being reported.
          var failureMessage: String? {
              if case .failed(let message) = phase { return message }
              return nil
          }
      
          /// The name to show for a trusted Mac, or nil when this device has never seen that ID —
          /// a Mac paired from somewhere else, or paired before names were being kept.
          func displayName(forHostID id: String) -> String? { hostNames[id] }
      
          /// When the session that is up now came up, for the elapsed-time readout. `nil` whenever
          /// there is no ready session.
          ///
          /// A `Date` and not a counter: the view formats it with `Text(_:style:.timer)`, which the
          /// system advances on its own. A `Timer` here would wake the main actor once a second to
          /// update a number that the screen can already count by itself.
          private(set) var sessionStartedAt: Date?
      
          /// Set when the device's own identity could not be loaded. Everything else is moot in
          /// that case: without a client certificate there is nothing for the Mac to pin.
          private(set) var identityFailure: String?
      
          // MARK: - User choices
      
          var manualAddress = "127.0.0.1"
          var manualPort = String(ProtocolInfo.defaultPort)
          private(set) var keyboardMode: KeyboardMode = .unicode
          private(set) var latchedModifiers: Modifiers = []
          private(set) var activeSourceID: String?
          var showKeyboard = false
          private(set) var typedPreview = ""
      
          // MARK: - Collaborators
      
          let renderer = VideoRenderer()
      
          private let pins = ClientPinStore.standard
          private let browser = HostBrowser()
          private let notifier = SessionNotifier.shared
      
          /// Whether the last thing Bonjour said was a failure.
          ///
          /// The browser replaces a dead one on its own, but a suspended app is not running to do it:
          /// the retry it had scheduled sits behind the app's suspension and only fires once the app
          /// is running again. Coming back to the foreground is the one moment worth restarting
          /// immediately rather than waiting that out.
          private var browseFailed = false
          private var identity: SelfSignedIdentity?
          private var device = DeviceIdentity(id: "", name: "")
          private var session: ClientSession?
          private var videoPoll: Task<Void, Never>?
      
          /// Set by the two ways the user ends a session themselves, read and cleared by the
          /// transition that follows.
          ///
          /// A dropped link and a deliberate end reach the model as the same phase, so intent has
          /// to be carried across rather than inferred — and it is carried no further than that
          /// transition, or a leftover flag would silence the news that the next session dropped.
          private var userEndedSession = false
      
          init() {
              device = DeviceIdentity.loadOrCreate(defaultName: UIDevice.current.name)
              pairedHostIDs = pins.hostIDs
              hostNames = UserDefaults.standard.dictionary(forKey: Self.hostNamesKey) as? [String: String] ?? [:]
              do {
                  identity = try SelfSignedIdentity.loadOrCreate(role: .client, commonName: device.name)
              } catch {
                  identityFailure = (error as? LocalizedError)?.errorDescription ?? "\(error)"
                  modelLog.error("could not load the client identity: \(String(describing: error), privacy: .public)")
              }
          }
      
          // MARK: - Discovery
      
          func start() {
              guard identityFailure == nil else { return }
              // Anything on the Lock Screen from a previous run describes a session this process did
              // not survive, and nothing else in this launch knows it is there.
              SessionActivity.shared.adoptOrphan()
              browser.onEvent = { [weak self] event in
                  // Bound once, outside the `Task`. A `weak self` reference is a mutable variable,
                  // and reading it from a closure that outlives this one is a data race the compiler
                  // is right to flag.
                  guard let self else { return }
                  // HostBrowser reports from its own queue. Every one of these touches observable
                  // state, so each is hopped deliberately rather than by luck.
                  Task { @MainActor in self.apply(event) }
              }
              browser.start()
          }
      
          func restartBrowsing() {
              browseStatus = "Looking for Macs on this network…"
              browser.stop()
              browser.start()
          }
      
          private func apply(_ event: HostBrowser.Event) {
              switch event {
              case .started:
                  browseFailed = false
                  browseStatus = "Looking for Macs on this network…"
              case .updated(let hosts):
                  browseFailed = false
                  self.hosts = hosts
                  if let pending = pendingHostID, let host = hosts.first(where: { $0.id == pending }) {
                      pendingHostID = nil
                      connect(to: .discovered(host))
                  }
                  self.resumeIfNeeded()
                  browseStatus = hosts.isEmpty
                      ? "No Macs found yet. Make sure Peering is running on your Mac and on the same network."
                      : "\(hosts.count) Mac\(hosts.count == 1 ? "" : "s") found"
              case .failed(let message):
                  // Bonjour failing is silent on iOS without the local-network permission and the
                  // NSBonjourServices entry, so the message is surfaced verbatim rather than
                  // smoothed over — the manual address path below is the way past it.
                  //
                  // Shown even though the browser is already replacing itself: the retry can take half
                  // a minute, and a status line that said nothing would leave the user looking at a
                  // list that has quietly stopped updating.
                  browseFailed = true
                  browseStatus = "Browsing failed: \(message)"
              }
          }
      
          // MARK: - Connecting
      
          /// Whether a session is up or on its way up. The same question as ``Phase/holdsSession`` —
          /// asked once, answered in one place.
          var isBusy: Bool { phase.holdsSession }
      
          func connect(to target: ClientSession.Target) {
              guard let identity, identityFailure == nil else { return }
      
              // Remembered for the home-screen widget, which can offer to connect but has no way of
              // knowing to what — see ``reconnectToLastHost()``. Written twice on purpose: the app
              // reads its own defaults, and the widget can only see the shared container.
              UserDefaults.standard.set(target.displayName, forKey: Self.lastHostNameKey)
              SharedStore.lastHostName = target.displayName
              // A widget is not a live view and is not told anything. Without this it goes on showing
              // the previous Mac until the system next feels like refreshing it, which on a widget
              // that changes twice a year could be tomorrow.
              WidgetCenter.shared.reloadAllTimelines()
      
              // Intent does not survive into the next attempt: a flag left over from a session the
              // user ended would otherwise suppress the news that its successor has dropped.
              userEndedSession = false
              // An attempt from the backoff timer would race this one and start a second session.
              stopReconnecting()
              // And a session that is already up must be torn down rather than replaced. Assigning
              // over it leaves the first connection running with nothing holding it, so the peer sees
              // it drop mid-handshake — which reads on the Mac as a clean disconnect and, with a retry
              // following it, is a loop rather than a session.
              session?.disconnect()
              session = nil
              // The user has just asked to reach a Mac, which is the first moment the question
              // "tell you when it needs you?" means anything.
              notifier.prepareForFirstConnect()
      
              hostName = target.displayName
              activeSourceID = nil
              catalog = nil
              notes.removeAll()
              videoStatus = "No video stream"
      
              let session = ClientSession(
                  identity: identity,
                  clientID: device.id,
                  clientName: device.name,
                  pins: pins,
                  onEvent: { [weak self] event in
                      guard let self else { return }
                      // **The video pipeline is the one event family that must not detour through
                      // the main actor**, and for `.config` that is a correctness rule rather than
                      // the performance one it is for `.frame`. At 60 Hz, hopping frames to the
                      // main actor would put 60 a second behind the layout of the view trying to
                      // draw them; hopping a config lets the frames overtake it.
                      //
                      // `ClientTransport` hands over everything it drained from one read in a
                      // single synchronous loop, so a config and the keyframe that follows it
                      // routinely arrive in the same batch. Send the config to the main actor and
                      // the keyframe wins the race: it is enqueued against the *previous* format
                      // description, and `configure` then flushes it away — the host's one
                      // guaranteed-decodable frame, discarded, leaving the client black until the
                      // encoder's next keyframe up to two seconds later. The renderer has its own
                      // serial queue, so both calls belong here, where their order is whatever the
                      // wire said it was.
                      //
                      // Reachable from here because `renderer` is a `let` of a `Sendable` type: an
                      // immutable property cannot race, so the actor boundary does not apply to
                      // reading it.
                      switch event {
                      case .video(.frame(let frame)):
                          self.renderer.enqueue(frame)
                          return
                      case .video(.config(let config)):
                          self.renderer.reset()
                          self.renderer.configure(config)
                      default:
                          break
                      }
                      Task { @MainActor in self.apply(event) }
                  }
              )
              self.session = session
              startVideoPolling()
      
              Task { await session.connect(to: target) }
          }
      
          func connectToManualAddress() {
              guard let port = UInt16(manualPort.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespaces)) else {
                  append(note: "“\(manualPort)” is not a port number.")
                  return
              }
              let host = manualAddress.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespaces)
              guard !host.isEmpty else { return }
      // CryptoKit is the system framework on Apple platforms; the open-source swift-crypto
      // module is named `Crypto`. Same API either way, so the package stays dependency-free
      // on Apple platforms without giving up portability.
      #if canImport(CryptoKit)
      import CryptoKit
      #else
      import Crypto
      #endif
      import Foundation
      import Network
      import Security
      import os
      
      private let sessionLog = Logger(subsystem: "pl.dmq.peering", category: "session")
      
      /// The client half of the MacCast protocol: connect, authenticate, and stay usable.
      ///
      /// This is the client's counterpart to the host's `HostSession`, and it is deliberately the
      /// same shape — a single state machine driven by frames from one connection, so the ordering
      /// guarantees the handshake depends on are enforced in exactly one place.
      ///
      /// Two sockets, always. ``control`` carries the handshake, commands, and the catalog;
      /// ``video`` carries nothing but encoded pictures. The split is not an optimisation: a
      /// single stream would put a 200 KB keyframe in front of the next mouse move, and cursor
      /// latency is the thing a user actually feels.
      public final class ClientSession: @unchecked Sendable {
          /// Where the session is in its life. Coarse on purpose — the UI renders this directly,
          /// so a finer state machine would just be a longer switch in the view.
          public enum Phase: Sendable, Equatable {
              case idle
              case connecting
              case handshaking
              /// Waiting for the human to compare six digits with the Mac's screen.
              case confirming(code: String)
              case ready
              case failed(String)
              case disconnected
      
              /// Whether a session is up, or on its way up, at this phase.
              ///
              /// A property of the state machine rather than of any one caller, and it lives here
              /// because three of them were asking it: the model, the notification policy, and the
              /// Live Activity. Three copies of a list of phases is three chances to update two of
              /// them when a state is added.
              public var holdsSession: Bool {
                  switch self {
                  case .connecting, .handshaking, .confirming, .ready: return true
                  case .idle, .failed, .disconnected: return false
                  }
              }
          }
      
          /// What the session tells its owner. Everything is a value, so the UI can apply these
          /// on whatever actor it likes.
          public enum Event: Sendable {
              case phase(Phase)
              case host(ServerHello)
              case catalog(CaptureCatalog)
              case video(VideoEvent)
              /// Round-trip time of a control ping, in milliseconds. The control channel is the
              /// one whose latency the user feels, so this is the number worth showing.
              case latency(milliseconds: Double)
              /// Diagnostics worth surfacing without failing: a pin that was accepted, a video
              /// channel that connected but has not produced a stream yet.
              case note(String)
          }
      
          public enum VideoEvent: Sendable {
              case connecting
              case config(VideoStreamConfig)
              case frame(EncodedVideoFrame)
              case ended(String)
          }
      
          /// How to reach a Mac. Both paths end in the same TLS + pairing handshake; they differ
          /// only in whether an address had to be resolved first.
          public enum Target: Sendable {
              /// Found over Bonjour. Carries the interface it was discovered on, which is the path
              /// that actually works on a Mac with several.
              case discovered(DiscoveredHost)
              /// A literal address. What the simulator needs, since Bonjour there is unreliable —
              /// and the honest fallback for a network that blocks multicast.
              case address(host: String, port: UInt16)
      
              public var displayName: String {
                  switch self {
                  case .discovered(let host): return host.name
                  case .address(let host, let port): return "\(host):\(port)"
                  }
              }
          }
      
          public enum Failure: LocalizedError, Sendable {
              case busy
              case notReady
              case protocolMismatch(client: UInt16, host: UInt16)
              case commitmentMismatch
              case noServerKey
              case pinMismatch(hostID: String)
              case unexpected(MessageKind, expected: String)
              case identity(String)
      
              public var errorDescription: String? {
                  switch self {
                  case .busy:
                      return "This session is already connecting or connected."
                  case .notReady:
                      return "The session is not connected."
                  case .protocolMismatch(let client, let host):
                      return "This Mac speaks protocol v\(host) and this app speaks v\(client). Update whichever is older."
                  case .commitmentMismatch:
                      // Reached only when a peer changed its contribution after seeing ours, which
                      // no honest implementation does.
                      return "The Mac's pairing reveal did not match its commitment."
                  case .noServerKey:
                      return "The Mac's certificate did not expose a public key, so it cannot be pinned."
                  case .pinMismatch(let hostID):
                      return "Something at this address is not the Mac you paired with (\(hostID)). Its key does not match the stored pin."
                  case .unexpected(let kind, let expected):
                      return "Expected \(expected) from the Mac, got \(kind)."
                  case .identity(let detail):
                      return "This device's identity could not be loaded: \(detail)"
                  }
              }
          }
      
          // MARK: - Configuration held for the session's life
      
          private let identity: SelfSignedIdentity
          private let clientID: String
          private let clientName: String
          private let pins: ClientPinStore
          private let onEvent: @Sendable (Event) -> Void
      
          /// The command queue, created once and reused across reconnects so a gesture in flight
          /// is not stranded by a reconnect. Its sink reads the current control connection under
          /// the lock, so a queued command can never be delivered to a dead socket.
          private let coalescer: CommandCoalescer
      
          // MARK: - State, all under `lock`
      
          private let lock = NSLock()
          private var _phase: Phase = .idle
          private var control: ClientConnection?
          private var video: ClientConnection?
          private var _serverHello: ServerHello?
          private var _catalog: CaptureCatalog?
          private var _serverKey: Data?
          private var state: HandshakeState = .idle
          private var pingTask: Task<Void, Never>?
          private var pingSentAt: DispatchTime?
      
          private var ephemeral: P256.KeyAgreement.PrivateKey?
          private var nonce: Data?
          private var remoteCommitment: Data?
      
          /// Where the handshake has got to. Separate from ``Phase`` because the UI does not need
          /// to distinguish "waiting for the server's commit" from "waiting for its reveal", but
          /// the state machine very much does.
          private enum HandshakeState {
              case idle
              case awaitingServerHello
              case awaitingServerCommit
              case awaitingServerReveal
              case awaitingUserConfirmation
              case awaitingPairResult
              case ready
              case failed
          }
      
          public init(
              identity: SelfSignedIdentity,
              clientID: String,
              clientName: String,
              pins: ClientPinStore = .standard,
              onEvent: @escaping @Sendable (Event) -> Void
          ) {
              self.identity = identity
              self.clientID = clientID
              self.clientName = clientName
              self.pins = pins
              self.onEvent = onEvent
      
              // `self` cannot be captured before every stored property is initialised, so the
              // coalescer is built with a closure that reads the connection through a box filled
              // in immediately afterwards. The alternative — making the whole class lazy — would
              // put a lock in the path of every cursor sample.
              let box = ConnectionBox()
              coalescer = CommandCoalescer(sink: { command in box.send(command) })
              box.attach(self)
          }
      
          deinit {
              pingTask?.cancel()
              coalescer.stop()
          }
      
          /// Holds the session weakly so the coalescer's sink can reach the live control
          /// connection without creating a retain cycle through the timer.
          private final class ConnectionBox: @unchecked Sendable {
              private let lock = NSLock()
              private weak var session: ClientSession?
      
              func attach(_ session: ClientSession) { lock.withLock { self.session = session } }
      
              func send(_ command: RemoteCommand) {
                  lock.withLock { session }?.sendNow(command)
              }
          }
      
          // MARK: - Observable state
      
          public var phase: Phase { lock.withLock { _phase } }
          public var serverHello: ServerHello? { lock.withLock { _serverHello } }
          public var catalog: CaptureCatalog? { lock.withLock { _catalog } }
          /// The Mac's identity key, from its TLS certificate.
          public var serverKey: Data? { lock.withLock { _serverKey } }
          public var isReady: Bool { lock.withLock { state == .ready } }
      
          // MARK: - Connect
      
          /// Runs the whole client side of the handshake and returns once the outcome is known:
          /// either the session is ready, or it has failed and the reason has been emitted.
          ///
          /// Returning rather than throwing is deliberate. Every failure already reaches the UI as
          /// a ``Phase/failed(_:)`` event, and a caller that also had to catch would have two
          /// places to render the same message — which is how one of them ends up stale.
          public func connect(to target: Target, timeout: TimeInterval = 10) async {
              guard beginConnecting() else {
                  emit(.phase(.failed(Failure.busy.errorDescription ?? "busy")))
                  return
              }
              emit(.phase(.connecting))
      
              let pinned: Data? = {
                  if case .discovered(let host) = target { return pins.pin(for: host.id) }
                  // A literal address says nothing about *which* Mac is at it, so there is no pin
                  // to insist on before the handshake. The post-handshake check below covers it.
                  return nil
              }()
      
              let connection = ClientConnection(label: "pl.dmq.peering.client.control")
              connection.onFrame = { [weak self] frame in self?.handle(frame) }
              connection.onClose = { [weak self] failure in self?.controlClosed(failure) }
              lock.withLock { control = connection }
      
              do {
                  switch target {
                  case .discovered(let host):
                      try await connection.connect(
                          to: host.endpoint,
                          identity: identity,
                          pinnedServerKey: pinned,
                          timeout: timeout
                      )
                  case .address(let host, let port):
                      try await connection.connect(
                          host: host,
                          port: port,
                          identity: identity,
                          pinnedServerKey: nil,
                          timeout: timeout
                      )
                  }
              } catch {
                  let message = (pinned != nil)
                      // A pin was in force and TLS refused, which is the one failure worth naming
                      // precisely: it is either an impostor or a Mac that was reset.
                      ? "The Mac at \(target.displayName) did not present the key this device has pinned for it. If it was reset, forget it here and pair again."
                      : (error as? LocalizedError)?.errorDescription ?? "\(error)"
                  fail(message)
                  return
              }
      
              lock.withLock { _serverKey = connection.observedServerKey }
              emit(.note("Connected over \(connection.negotiatedTLSVersion)"))
      
              // 1. Declare the role. One listener serves both channels, and this is what tells the
              //    Mac which one it just accepted.
              connection.send(Frame(
                  kind: .connectionRole,
                  payload: Data([ConnectionRole.control.rawValue])
              ))

              //    Mac knows its own pin store.

                  interfaces[host.id, default: 0] += 1
                  guard byID[host.id] == nil else { continue }
                  byID[host.id] = host
                  order.append(host.id)
              }
      
              return order.compactMap { id in
                  guard let host = byID[id] else { return nil }

                      id: host.id,
                      name: host.name,
                      endpoint: host.endpoint,
                      protocolVersion: host.protocolVersion,
                      interfaceCount: interfaces[id] ?? 1

          func start() {

              // not survive, and nothing else in this launch knows it is there.

              browser.stop()

              case .updated(let hosts):

                      pendingHostID = nil
                      connect(to: .discovered(host))
                  }
                  self.resumeIfNeeded()
                  browseStatus = hosts.isEmpty
                      ? "No Macs found yet. Make sure Peering is running on your Mac and on the same network."

                  // a minute, and a status line that said nothing would leave the user looking at a
                  // list that has quietly stopped updating.

              // reads its own defaults, and the widget can only see the shared container.
              UserDefaults.standard.set(target.displayName, forKey: Self.lastHostNameKey)
              SharedStore.lastHostName = target.displayName
              // A widget is not a live view and is not told anything. Without this it goes on showing
              // the previous Mac until the system next feels like refreshing it, which on a widget
              // that changes twice a year could be tomorrow.
              WidgetCenter.shared.reloadAllTimelines()
      
              // Intent does not survive into the next attempt: a flag left over from a session the
              // user ended would otherwise suppress the news that its successor has dropped.
              userEndedSession = false
              // An attempt from the backoff timer would race this one and start a second session.
              stopReconnecting()
              // And a session that is already up must be torn down rather than replaced. Assigning
              // over it leaves the first connection running with nothing holding it, so the peer sees
              // it drop mid-handshake — which reads on the Mac as a clean disconnect and, with a retry
              // following it, is a loop rather than a session.
              session?.disconnect()
              session = nil

              // "tell you when it needs you?" means anything.
              notifier.prepareForFirstConnect()
      
              hostName = target.displayName
              activeSourceID = nil
              catalog = nil
              notes.removeAll()
              videoStatus = "No video stream"

                  identity: identity,
                  clientID: device.id,
                  clientName: device.name,
                  pins: pins,

                      guard let self else { return }
                      // **The video pipeline is the one event family that must not detour through
                      // the main actor**, and for `.config` that is a correctness rule rather than
                      // the performance one it is for `.frame`. At 60 Hz, hopping frames to the
                      // main actor would put 60 a second behind the layout of the view trying to
                      // draw them; hopping a config lets the frames overtake it.
                      //
                      // `ClientTransport` hands over everything it drained from one read in a
                      // single synchronous loop, so a config and the keyframe that follows it
                      // routinely arrive in the same batch. Send the config to the main actor and
                      // the keyframe wins the race: it is enqueued against the *previous* format
                      // description, and `configure` then flushes it away — the host's one
                      // guaranteed-decodable frame, discarded, leaving the client black until the
                      // encoder's next keyframe up to two seconds later. The renderer has its own
                      // serial queue, so both calls belong here, where their order is whatever the
                      // wire said it was.
                      //
                      // Reachable from here because `renderer` is a `let` of a `Sendable` type: an

          func connectToManualAddress() {

                  return
              }
              let host = manualAddress.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespaces)
              guard !host.isEmpty else { return }
              connect(to: .address(host: host, port: port))

          private func apply(_ event: ClientSession.Event) {

                  // the point the stopwatch starts from — is about where the session came from,
                  // not only about where it landed.

                  self.phase = phase

                      videoStatus = "Stopped: \(message)"
                  }
                  if phase == .disconnected {
                      videoStatus = "Disconnected"
                  }
                  if phase == .ready {
                      // Restarted on every fresh arrival rather than only the first: a reconnect
                      // emits `.ready` again, and elapsed time that kept counting through it would
                      // be describing a session that no longer exists.
                      if previous != .ready {

                          // failure a retry cannot fix spends its five attempts and then stops

                          reconnectAttempt = 0
                          sessionStartedAt = Date()

                          // a connect that failed halfway is not something to restore.
                          UserDefaults.standard.set(true, forKey: Self.resumeKey)

                  }

                  userEndedSession = false

                      from: previous,
                      to: phase,
                      hostName: hostName ?? "the Mac",
                      deliberate: userEnded
                  )

                  // from another app, and once as something they will see without unlocking. Neither
                  // is a substitute for the other, and both read from this one place.
                  // A session that ended without the user asking is put back on its own. The flag
                  // inside `scheduleReconnect` is what decides whether this was theirs — the phase
                  // alone cannot tell a drop from a disconnect.
                  //
                  // Before the activity is told, not after: scheduling is what sets `isReconnecting`,
                  // and the card has to go up saying "reconnecting" rather than be taken down and
                  // brought back a moment later as though nothing had happened.
                  if !phase.holdsSession, !userEnded {
                      scheduleReconnect()
                  }
                  SessionActivity.shared.sessionMoved(
                      from: previous,
                      to: phase,
                      hostName: hostName ?? "the Mac",
                      startedAt: sessionStartedAt,
                      reconnecting: isReconnecting
                  )
      
                  if !phase.holdsSession {

                      // gone. Nothing else can: the release would have to travel back over the same
                      // connection. Observed on this Mac, the window server keeps the flag until a

                      // says so rather than quietly showing the buttons as released.

                      hostNames[hello.serverID] = hello.hostName

                  }

                  self.catalog = catalog
                  if activeSourceID == nil, let first = catalog.displays.first ?? catalog.all.first {
                      activeSourceID = first.id
                  }
              case .video(let event):
                  apply(video: event)
              case .latency(let milliseconds):
                  latencyMilliseconds = milliseconds
              case .note(let message):
                  append(note: message)
              }
          }
      
          private func apply(video event: ClientSession.VideoEvent) {
              switch event {
              case .connecting:
                  videoStatus = "Opening the video channel…"
              case .config(let config):
                  // The decoder half of this is done on the network queue, in the same place the
                  // frames are handled, so that it is ordered against them — see the event handler
                  // in `connect(to:)`. Flushing and reconfiguring here instead would put the reset
                  // *after* a keyframe that arrived in the same read, and throw that keyframe away.
                  // Only the labels belong on the main actor.
                  videoStatus = "\(config.codec.rawValue.uppercased()) \(config.pixelWidth)×\(config.pixelHeight)"
                  append(note: "Video stream started: \(config.pixelWidth)×\(config.pixelHeight) \(config.codec.rawValue.uppercased())")
              case .frame:
                  break // Handled on the network queue; see `connect(to:)`.
              case .ended(let reason):
                  videoStatus = "Video ended: \(reason)"
              }
          }
      
          private func startVideoPolling() {
              videoPoll?.cancel()
              videoPoll = Task { [weak self] in
                  while !Task.isCancelled {
                      try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(500))
                      guard let self else { return }
                      let snapshot = self.renderer.currentSnapshot
                      if snapshot.hasConfig {
                          let suffix = snapshot.framesDropped > 0 ? " · \(snapshot.framesDropped) dropped" : ""
                          let waiting = snapshot.awaitingKeyframe ? " · waiting for a keyframe" : ""
                          self.videoStatus = "\(snapshot.codec.rawValue.uppercased()) \(snapshot.pixelWidth)×\(snapshot.pixelHeight) · \(snapshot.framesEnqueued) frames\(suffix)\(waiting)"
                      }
                  }
              }
          }
      
          private func append(note: String) {
              notes.append(note)
              if notes.count > 12 { notes.removeFirst(notes.count - 12) }
          }
      
          // MARK: - Pairing
      
          func confirmPairing(accepted: Bool) {
              // Declining ends the session from the Mac's side too, and that arrives as a
              // `.disconnected` like any other — with the model's phase still on `.confirming`.
              // Without this the user's own "no" comes back to them as a lost connection.
              if !accepted { userEndedSession = true }
              session?.confirmPairing(accepted: accepted)
          }
      
          /// Ends the session now.
          ///
          /// `deliberate` answers "did the user mean to do this", which is not the same question as
          /// "who called this function". A disconnect the user tapped is silent; one iOS forced
          /// because it is about to suspend the app is not, because they are looking at something else
          /// and a banner is the only way they will ever hear about it.
          func disconnect(deliberate: Bool = true) {
              // Recorded before anything moves. `ClientSession` announces the end itself, and by
              // the time that event is applied the phase below has already been set — so this flag
              // is the only evidence left that the user, and not the network, ended it.
              userEndedSession = deliberate
              // Only a deliberate one. A drop, and the end iOS forces on a backgrounded app, are the
              // two cases where coming back to the app should find the session restored.
              if deliberate {
                  UserDefaults.standard.set(false, forKey: Self.resumeKey)
                  stopReconnecting()
              }
              sessionStartedAt = nil
              session?.disconnect()
              session = nil
              videoPoll?.cancel()
              videoPoll = nil
              renderer.reset()
              latchedModifiers = []
              phase = .disconnected
          }

          /// Whether a trusted Mac has been asked for and not yet found.

          /// Connects to a Mac this device has paired with before, by ID.

          /// interface it was seen on, and a remembered address would be the wrong one the moment the
          /// network changed. What this saves is the *second* tap — the request is remembered and acted
          /// on the moment the Mac appears, instead of the user staring at an empty list, deciding it
          /// did not work, and trying again.
          func connectToTrusted(hostID: String) {
              if let host = hosts.first(where: { $0.id == hostID }) {
                  pendingHostID = nil
                  connect(to: .discovered(host))
                  return
              }
              pendingHostID = hostID
          }

          /// Where the name of the last Mac this device connected to is kept.
      import AppKit
      import Foundation
      import Observation
      import RemoteCore
      import os
      
      /// Host diagnostics, visible with:
      /// `log stream --predicate 'subsystem == "pl.dmq.peering.host"'`
      ///
      /// The window is not always reachable — a headless run, a background launch, a user who
      /// cannot see the screen — and every failure mode in this app is silent by nature. Logging
      /// to the unified log means "the client connected but nothing happened" is answerable
      /// without a debugger.
      private let hostLog = Logger(subsystem: "pl.dmq.peering.host", category: "session")
      
      /// Main-actor state for the host window.
      ///
      /// The networking layer knows nothing about SwiftUI and emits ``HostEvent`` values from a
      /// background queue; this type is the single place those cross back to the main actor.
      /// Keeping that hop in one file means the session state machine never has to reason about
      /// actor isolation, and there is exactly one `Task { @MainActor }` to audit rather than a
      /// scattering of them.
      @MainActor
      @Observable
      final class HostModel {
          enum Status: Equatable {
              case idle
              case starting
              case listening(port: UInt16)
              case failed(String)
      
              var isListening: Bool {
                  if case .listening = self { return true }
                  return false
              }
          }
      
          private(set) var status: Status = .idle
          private(set) var deviceName = ""
          private(set) var deviceID = ""
      
          /// Present only while a first-time pairing is waiting on the user's comparison.
          private(set) var pairing: PairingPrompt?
          private(set) var lastOutcome: PairingOutcome?
      
          private(set) var connectedClients: [ConnectedClient] = []
          private(set) var pairedClientIDs: [String] = []
      
          /// Whether a given trusted device is attached right now.
          ///
          /// Matched on the ID, which is the only thing the two lists have in common. The name is the
          /// client's to choose, two devices can present the same one, and comparing it against a list
          /// of IDs is a question that is always false — which is how a connected iPhone came to read
          /// as merely "Trusted".
          func isConnected(_ id: String) -> Bool {

          private func launchApplication(bundleIdentifier: String) {

                    bundleIdentifier.unicodeScalars.allSatisfy({ allowed.contains($0) }),
                    let url = NSWorkspace.shared.urlForApplication(withBundleIdentifier: bundleIdentifier)

              configuration.activates = true
              NSWorkspace.shared.openApplication(at: url, configuration: configuration) { [weak self] application, error in

                      guard let self else { return }

                          self.record("Could not launch application: \(error.localizedDescription)")
                          return
                      }
                      guard let application else {
                          self.record("Application launched but no running process was returned")
                          return

          private func switchToLaunchedApplication(_ application: NSRunningApplication) {

                  record("Application opened; capture is not connected")
                  return

              pendingCaptureSource = source

              // observable result instead of assuming that the process being alive means SCK has it.
              Task { [weak self, weak coordinator] in
                  guard let self, let coordinator else { return }
                  var lastError: Error?
                  for attempt in 0..<20 {
                      do {
                          try await coordinator.switchSource(source)
                          await MainActor.run { self.pendingCaptureSource = nil }
                          return
                      } catch {
                          lastError = error
                          if attempt < 19 {
                              try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(150))
                          }
                      }
                  }
                  let message = (lastError as? LocalizedError)?.errorDescription
                      ?? lastError.map(String.init(describing:))
                      ?? "The application did not expose a capturable window."
                  await MainActor.run { self.record("Could not switch to application: \(message)") }
              }
          }

                  record("All paired clients removed")

      `Environment=` lines go in `/etc/peeringd.env`, which keeps the unit readable and the settings
      greppable. Binding 443 directly needs `AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`; shape B does not,
      since nginx owns that port.
      
      The binary is static with no runtime dependencies, so an update is a file replacement:
      
      ```sh
      systemctl stop peeringd
      scp peeringd-linux-x86_64 server:/usr/local/bin/peeringd
      ssh server 'chmod +x /usr/local/bin/peeringd && systemctl start peeringd'
      ```
      
      Restarting drops live sessions and both ends reconnect on their own — the Mac re-registers, the
      phone asks again. Worth doing when nobody is mid-session anyway.
      
      #### One limitation worth knowing
      
      Shape B gets signalling onto 443, but **control still needs 9443**. Some corporate and hotel
      networks allow only 80 and 443 outbound, so the app will find the Mac and then fail to open the
      control connection. Cellular and home networks are unaffected, which covers the intended use, but
      it is a real edge and worth recognising from the symptom rather than debugging from scratch.
      
      Bandwidth is the only real running cost: see the note below.
      
      ## The wire contract
      
      Everything below is what the Swift side implements. Hex means lowercase hex of 16 raw bytes.
      
      ### Signalling — WebSocket, JSON
      
      A **Mac** sends `registerHost` and then simply holds the socket open. Holding it open *is* its
      presence: there is no heartbeat and no roster, so a Mac that drops is offline the moment the socket
      closes, and re-registers when it comes back — on a new address, under the same device ID.
      
      ```jsonc
      // Mac → relay
      {"type":"registerHost","deviceId":"…","name":"Studio","protocolVersion":3}
      // relay → Mac
      {"type":"registered","sessionTtlSeconds":300}
      
      // phone → relay
      {"type":"connectToHost","hostId":"…","clientId":"…","protocolVersion":3}
      ```
      
      `clientId` is the phone's own device ID. The relay wants it only to recognise a reconnecting phone
      and supersede its previous session rather than accumulate one per attempt.
      
      Both ends then receive a session. **This is the one message the two ends do not receive
      identically** — the `videoToken` differs, for the reason given under video below.
      
      ```jsonc
      {"type":"sessionReady","controlHost":"…","controlPort":9443,"videoHost":"…","videoPort":51234,
       "controlToken":"…","videoToken":"…"}
      ```
      
      The Mac receives it unsolicited — it never asked for this, and a phone may connect to it at any
      time. If the Mac is not registered, the phone gets:
      
      ```jsonc
      {"type":"hostOffline","deviceId":"…"}
      ```
      
      `{"type":"ping"}` keeps an idle socket alive through NAT timeouts and is answered with
      `{"type":"pong"}`. Anything unparseable is answered with `{"type":"error","code":…,"message":…}`.
      
      ### Control — TCP
      
      Connect to `controlHost:controlPort`, write the **16 raw bytes** `unhex(controlToken)` with no
      framing and no newline, then start TLS immediately. The relay consumes exactly those 16 bytes and
      splices the rest to the peer verbatim; everything after them belongs to the two ends.
      
      The token is single-use and is spent when the splice it paid for finishes. It travels in the clear
      because it has to: it is what tells the relay where to carry the handshake, so it necessarily
      precedes it. Stealing one buys an attacker a connection that fails its handshake.
      
      ### Video — UDP
      
      Send a bind packet to `videoHost:videoPort`:
      
      ```
        4 bytes        16 bytes
        "PBND"     ‖   unhex(videoToken)
      ```
      
      Then send and receive video datagrams on the same socket. Anything from an unbound address is
      dropped **without a reply**, so a prober learns nothing about whether a session exists.
      
      **Each end has a different token, and that is load-bearing.** With one shared token the relay could
      not tell which slot a re-bind belonged to, so a phone whose carrier NAT moved it mid-session would
      be indistinguishable from a stranger taking a slot, and slot assignment would depend on which
      packet happened to arrive first. Two tokens fix the mapping — slot 0 is always the phone, slot 1 is

      //! that both travelled outbound find each other.
      //!

      //! endpoints belong together", and nothing here decides whether they are *allowed* to talk. That
      //! decision is made by the two ends themselves, in the TLS handshake and the pin that follows it,
      //! and it is the only reason this relay can be a dumb forwarder without being a security hole.
      //!
      //! A direct consequence, and one worth being explicit about: the control token is not a secret.
      //! It has to be presented in the clear before TLS starts, because TLS is what it is carrying. All
      //! it does is claim a place in a splice; someone who steals it gets a connection that fails its
      //! handshake.

                  .sessions
                  .retain(|_, session| session.last_activity.elapsed() < ttl);
              before - inner.sessions.len()
          }
      
          pub async fn len(&self) -> usize {
              self.inner.lock().await.sessions.len()
          }
      
          pub async fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
              self.len().await == 0
          }
      
          /// For tests and logs: the client's video token belonging to a control token.
          pub async fn video_token_for(&self, token: &Token) -> Option<Token> {
              self.inner
                  .lock()
                  .await
                  .sessions
                  .get(token)
                  .map(|session| session.video_tokens[CLIENT_SLOT])
          }
      }
      
      #[cfg(test)]
      mod tests {
          use super::*;
          use std::net::Ipv4Addr;
      
          const CLIENT: Token = [1u8; 16];
          const HOST: Token = [2u8; 16];
      
          fn addr(last: u8, port: u16) -> SocketAddr {
              SocketAddr::from((Ipv4Addr::new(127, 0, 0, last), port))
          }
      
          fn pairing() -> VideoPairing {
              VideoPairing::new([CLIENT, HOST])
          }
      
          #[test]
          fn each_end_gets_its_own_slot_regardless_of_who_binds_first() {
              // The host sends its bind packet first, and still lands in slot 1. Slot assignment follows
              // the token, not arrival order — otherwise "slot 0" in a log would mean the phone or the
              // Mac depending on which packet won a race, and there would be no way to tell which.
              let mut video = pairing();
              assert_eq!(video.bind(&HOST, addr(2, 6000)), Some(1));
              assert_eq!(video.bind(&CLIENT, addr(1, 5000)), Some(0));
              assert!(video.is_complete());
      
              assert_eq!(video.peer_of(&addr(1, 5000)), Some(addr(2, 6000)));
              assert_eq!(video.peer_of(&addr(2, 6000)), Some(addr(1, 5000)));
          }
      
          #[test]
          fn a_rebinding_end_keeps_its_slot_and_moves_its_address() {
              // The case this exists for: a carrier NAT moves the phone's mapping mid-session. It
              // re-sends its bind packet from the new address and is reachable again — without becoming
              // a third participant and without displacing the Mac. This is the one failure the video
              // path cannot recover from by reconnecting, because there is no connection to re-establish.
              let mut video = pairing();
              video.bind(&CLIENT, addr(1, 5000));
              video.bind(&HOST, addr(2, 6000));
      
              assert_eq!(video.bind(&CLIENT, addr(1, 7000)), Some(0), "same slot, new address");
              assert_eq!(video.peer_of(&addr(1, 7000)), Some(addr(2, 6000)));
              assert_eq!(video.peer_of(&addr(2, 6000)), Some(addr(1, 7000)), "the host follows");
              assert_eq!(
                  video.peer_of(&addr(1, 5000)),
                  None,
                  "the old mapping is gone, not a second participant"
              );
          }
      
          #[test]
          fn a_token_can_only_move_its_own_slot() {
              // Presenting the Mac's token moves the Mac. It does not let whoever holds it take the
              // client's slot, which one shared token could not have expressed.
              let mut video = pairing();
              video.bind(&CLIENT, addr(1, 5000));
              video.bind(&HOST, addr(2, 6000));
      
              assert_eq!(video.bind(&HOST, addr(3, 7000)), Some(1));
              assert_eq!(video.peer_of(&addr(1, 5000)), Some(addr(3, 7000)));
              assert_eq!(video.peer_of(&addr(3, 7000)), Some(addr(1, 5000)));
          }
      
          #[test]
          fn a_token_that_was_never_issued_binds_nothing() {
              let mut video = pairing();
              assert_eq!(video.bind(&[9u8; 16], addr(1, 5000)), None);
              assert_eq!(video.peer_of(&addr(1, 5000)), None);
          }
      
          #[test]
          fn an_unknown_source_has_no_peer_and_does_not_get_a_reply() {
              let mut video = pairing();
              video.bind(&CLIENT, addr(1, 5000));
      
              assert_eq!(video.peer_of(&addr(9, 9999)), None);
          }
      
          #[tokio::test]
          async fn allocate_hands_out_distinct_tokens() {
              let registry = Registry::new();
              let a = registry.allocate("mac", "phone").await;
              let b = registry.allocate("mac", "other-phone").await;
      
              assert_ne!(a.control_token, b.control_token);
              assert_ne!(a.video_tokens, b.video_tokens);
              // And the two ends of one session do not share theirs either. That is what makes a re-bind
              // unambiguous, and it is why the two `SessionReady` messages differ.
              assert_ne!(a.video_tokens[CLIENT_SLOT], a.video_tokens[HOST_SLOT]);
              assert_eq!(registry.len().await, 2);
          }
      
          #[tokio::test]
          async fn reallocating_for_the_same_pair_supersedes_the_old_session() {
              let registry = Registry::new();
              let first = registry.allocate("mac", "phone").await;
              let second = registry.allocate("mac", "phone").await;
      
              assert_eq!(registry.len().await, 1, "one phone, one Mac, one session");
              assert!(registry.video_token_for(&first.control_token).await.is_none());
              assert!(registry.video_token_for(&second.control_token).await.is_some());
          }
      
          #[tokio::test]
          async fn the_first_connection_waits_and_the_second_hands_itself_over() {
              let registry = Registry::new();
              let allocated = registry.allocate("mac", "phone").await;
              let token = allocated.control_token;
      
              // Stand-ins for the two live sockets; the pairing logic only moves them around.
              let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0").await.unwrap();
              let listener_addr = listener.local_addr().unwrap();
              let first_socket = TcpStream::connect(listener_addr).await.unwrap();
              let second_socket = TcpStream::connect(listener_addr).await.unwrap();
      
              let first = registry.join_control(&token, first_socket).await;
              let second = registry.join_control(&token, second_socket).await;
              assert!(matches!(second, Some(Join::HandedOver)));
      
              // The side that arrived first keeps its own stream and receives the side that arrived
              // second, so it holds both halves and can splice them. Getting this wrong — moving our own
              // stream into the channel and never getting it back — leaves the waiter with one half and
              // nothing to splice it to, which is exactly what this asserts against.
              let Some(Join::Waiting { mine, peer }) = first else {
                  panic!("the first connection should be the one waiting");
              };
              assert!(mine.peer_addr().is_ok(), "the waiter keeps its own stream");
              assert!(peer.await.is_ok(), "the peer's stream should arrive");
          }
      
          #[tokio::test]
          async fn a_token_that_was_never_issued_joins_nothing() {
              let registry = Registry::new();
              let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0").await.unwrap();
              let socket = TcpStream::connect(listener.local_addr().unwrap()).await.unwrap();
      
              assert!(registry.join_control(&[0xff; 16], socket).await.is_none());
          }
      
          #[tokio::test]
          async fn releasing_a_session_makes_its_token_useless() {
              let registry = Registry::new();
              let allocated = registry.allocate("mac", "phone").await;
              registry.release(&allocated.control_token).await;
      
              let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0").await.unwrap();
              let socket = TcpStream::connect(listener.local_addr().unwrap()).await.unwrap();
              assert!(registry
                  .join_control(&allocated.control_token, socket)
                  .await
                  .is_none());
          }
      
          #[tokio::test]
          async fn the_sweep_takes_abandoned_sessions_and_leaves_busy_ones() {
              let registry = Registry::new();
              registry.allocate("mac", "phone").await;
      
              assert_eq!(registry.sweep(Duration::from_secs(300)).await, 0);
              assert_eq!(registry.sweep(Duration::ZERO).await, 1);
              assert!(registry.is_empty().await);
          }

      /// Handles one client message, returning the reply to send back to *this* connection.
      async fn dispatch(
          message: ClientMessage,
          self_tx: &mpsc::Sender<ServerMessage>,
          registry: &Arc<Registry>,
          hosts: &HostRegistry,
          settings: &Settings,
          relay_host: &str,
          registered_as: &mut Option<String>,
      ) -> Option<ServerMessage> {
          match message {
              ClientMessage::RegisterHost {
                  device_id,
                  name,
                  protocol_version,
              } => {
                  hosts
                      .put(&device_id, name.clone(), protocol_version, self_tx.clone())
                      .await;
                  *registered_as = Some(device_id.clone());
                  info!(%device_id, %name, protocol_version, "host registered");
                  Some(ServerMessage::Registered {
                      session_ttl_seconds: settings.session_ttl.as_secs(),
                  })
              }
      
              ClientMessage::ConnectToHost {
                  host_id,
                  client_id,
                  protocol_version,
              } => {
                  let Some(host) = hosts.entry_for(&host_id).await else {
                      debug!(%host_id, "asked for a host that is not registered");
                      return Some(ServerMessage::HostOffline { device_id: host_id });
                  };
      
                  // Checked here so a mismatched pair is told before either end spends a round trip on a
                  // handshake that would fail anyway. The two ends check it again themselves — this is a
                  // courtesy, not the enforcement.
                  if host.protocol_version != protocol_version {
                      return Some(ServerMessage::error(
                          "version",
                          format!(
                              "host speaks v{}, client speaks v{protocol_version}",
                              host.protocol_version
                          ),
                      ));
                  }
      
                  let allocated = registry.allocate(&host_id, &client_id).await;
      
                  let video_port = match udp_relay::serve_session(
                      settings.video_bind,
                      Arc::clone(&settings.video_ports),
                      Arc::clone(&allocated.video),
                      allocated.shutdown,
                      settings.session_ttl,
                  )
                  .await
                  {
                      Ok(port) => port,
                      Err(error) => {
                          warn!(%error, "could not bind a video socket");
                          return Some(ServerMessage::error("relay", "no video port available"));
                      }
                  };
      
                  // The name is here because it is the one thing that makes this log line useful to
                  // whoever is running the relay: a device ID identifies a machine to a database, and a
                  // name identifies it to a person reading `journalctl`.
                  info!(%host_id, host_name = %host.name, %client_id, video_port, "session allocated");
      
                  // The two ends get *different* video tokens, which is the one place the messages they
                  // receive diverge. See `VideoPairing` for why a shared token cannot express a re-bind.
                  // The control token is shared because it is presented once by each side and used up.
                  let ready = |video_token: Token| ServerMessage::SessionReady {
                      control_host: relay_host.to_string(),
                      control_port: settings.public_control_port,
                      video_host: relay_host.to_string(),
                      // The bound port unless it has been said otherwise, which is the case on a shared
                      // address where the forwarded port is the host's to choose.
                      video_port: settings.public_video_port.unwrap_or(video_port),
                      control_token: hex(&allocated.control_token),
                      video_token: hex(&video_token),
                  };
      
                  // Pushed to the Mac first. It did not ask for this, so a failure here means the Mac has
                  // gone away between registering and now — reported to the phone rather than leaving it
                  // waiting on a session the other end will never join.
                  if host
                      .tx
                      .send(ready(allocated.video_tokens[HOST_SLOT]))
                      .await
                      .is_err()
                  {
                      debug!(%host_id, "host push failed");
                      registry.release(&allocated.control_token).await;
                      return Some(ServerMessage::HostOffline { device_id: host_id });
                  }
      
                  Some(ready(allocated.video_tokens[CLIENT_SLOT]))
              }
      
              ClientMessage::Ping => Some(ServerMessage::Pong),
          }
      }

## Assistant

The first hard incompatibility is now clear: the relay speaks protocol v3 while `RemoteCore` still declares v2. The second is transport-level: the 16-byte routing token must be written before the existing end-to-end TLS handshake on the same TCP socket. I’m checking Apple’s local Network framework interface to choose a supported pre-TLS mechanism; this is the part where guessing would produce a client that never gets past the relay.
