      public enum RelayTunnelError: LocalizedError, Sendable, Equatable {
          case invalidPort(UInt16)
          case listener(String)
          case transport(String)
      
          public var errorDescription: String? {
              switch self {
              case .invalidPort(let port): return "The relay supplied an invalid control port: \(port)."
              case .listener(let message): return "Could not open the local relay tunnel: \(message)"
              case .transport(let message): return "The relay control tunnel failed: \(message)"
              }
          }
      }
      
      /// Presents a loopback TCP endpoint backed by a routed socket to `peeringd`.
      ///
      /// The existing client TLS transport connects to the loopback endpoint and still owns the TLS
      /// handshake end to end. The proxy writes the relay's 16-byte routing token first, then copies the
      /// opaque TLS bytes. This avoids teaching the security state machine anything about rendezvous.
      public final class RelayControlProxy: @unchecked Sendable {
          private let queue = DispatchQueue(label: "pl.dmq.peering.relay.client-tunnel")
          private let session: RelaySession
          private var listener: NWListener?
          private var splice: RelayByteSplice?
      
          public init(session: RelaySession) {
              self.session = session
          }
      
          public func start() async throws -> NWEndpoint {
              guard session.controlToken.count == 16 else { throw RelayProtocolError.invalidToken }
              let listener: NWListener
              do {
                  let parameters = NWParameters.tcp
                  parameters.allowLocalEndpointReuse = true
                  listener = try NWListener(using: parameters, on: .any)
              } catch {
                  throw RelayTunnelError.listener(error.localizedDescription)
              }
              self.listener = listener
      
              return try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { continuation in
                  let resumed = OneShotContinuation(continuation)
                  listener.stateUpdateHandler = { [weak self] state in
                      guard let self else { return }
                      switch state {
                      case .ready:
                          guard let port = listener.port else {
                              resumed.resume(throwing: RelayTunnelError.listener("No local port was assigned."))
                              return
                          }
                          resumed.resume(returning: .hostPort(host: "127.0.0.1", port: port))
                      case .failed(let error):
                          resumed.resume(throwing: RelayTunnelError.listener(error.localizedDescription))
                          self.cancel()
                      case .cancelled:
                          resumed.resume(throwing: RelayTunnelError.listener("The local listener stopped."))
                      default:
                          break
                      }
                  }
                  listener.newConnectionHandler = { [weak self] local in
                      guard let self else { local.cancel(); return }
                      self.listener?.newConnectionHandler = nil
                      self.listener?.cancel()
                      self.listener = nil
                      do {
                          let splice = try RelayByteSplice(
                              local: local,
                              relayHost: self.session.controlHost,
                              relayPort: self.session.controlPort,
                              token: self.session.controlToken,
                              queue: self.queue
                          )
                          self.splice = splice
                          splice.start()
                      } catch {
                          local.cancel()
                      }
                  }
                  listener.start(queue: queue)
              }
          }
      
          public func cancel() {
              queue.async { [self] in
                  listener?.cancel()
                  listener = nil
                  splice?.cancel()
                  splice = nil
              }
          }
      }
      
      /// Copies a relay socket to a local TCP endpoint. The host points this at its existing TLS
      /// listener, which preserves the crucial server role even though its internet socket is outbound.
      public final class RelayControlBridge: @unchecked Sendable {
          private let splice: RelayByteSplice
      
          public init(
              session: RelaySession,
              localPort: UInt16,
              onClose: (@Sendable () -> Void)? = nil
          ) throws {
              guard let port = NWEndpoint.Port(rawValue: localPort) else {
                  throw RelayTunnelError.invalidPort(localPort)
              }
              let local = NWConnection(to: .hostPort(host: "127.0.0.1", port: port), using: .tcp)
              splice = try RelayByteSplice(
                  local: local,
                  relayHost: session.controlHost,
                  relayPort: session.controlPort,
                  token: session.controlToken,
                  queue: DispatchQueue(label: "pl.dmq.peering.relay.host-tunnel"),
                  onStop: onClose
              )
          }
      
          public func start() { splice.start() }
          public func cancel() { splice.cancel() }
      }
      
      private final class OneShotContinuation<Value: Sendable>: @unchecked Sendable {
          private let lock = NSLock()
          private var continuation: CheckedContinuation<Value, any Error>?
      
          init(_ continuation: CheckedContinuation<Value, any Error>) {
              self.continuation = continuation
          }
      
          func resume(returning value: Value) {
              lock.withLock {
                  continuation?.resume(returning: value)
                  continuation = nil
              }
          }
      
          func resume(throwing error: any Error) {
              lock.withLock {
                  continuation?.resume(throwing: error)
                  continuation = nil
              }
          }
      }
      
      /// Backpressured, bidirectional byte copying. All state lives on `queue`.
      private final class RelayByteSplice: @unchecked Sendable {
          private let local: NWConnection
          private let relay: NWConnection
          private let token: Data
          private let queue: DispatchQueue
          private let onStop: (@Sendable () -> Void)?
          private var localReady = false
          private var relayReady = false
          private var tokenSent = false
          private var pumping = false
          private var stopped = false
      
          init(
              local: NWConnection,
              relayHost: String,
              relayPort: UInt16,
              token: Data,
              queue: DispatchQueue,
              onStop: (@Sendable () -> Void)? = nil
          ) throws {
              guard let port = NWEndpoint.Port(rawValue: relayPort) else {
                  throw RelayTunnelError.invalidPort(relayPort)
              }
              self.local = local
              relay = NWConnection(to: .hostPort(host: NWEndpoint.Host(relayHost), port: port), using: .tcp)
              self.token = token
              self.queue = queue
              self.onStop = onStop
          }
      
          func start() {
              local.stateUpdateHandler = { [weak self] state in self?.state(state, isLocal: true) }
              relay.stateUpdateHandler = { [weak self] state in self?.state(state, isLocal: false) }
              local.start(queue: queue)
              relay.start(queue: queue)
          }
      
          func cancel() {
              queue.async { [self] in stop() }
          }
      
          private func state(_ state: NWConnection.State, isLocal: Bool) {
              switch state {
              case .ready:
                  if isLocal { localReady = true } else { relayReady = true }
                  advance()
              case .failed, .cancelled:
                  stop()
              default:
                  break
              }
          }
      
          private func advance() {
              guard !stopped, localReady, relayReady else { return }
              guard !tokenSent else {
                  guard !pumping else { return }
                  pumping = true
                  pump(from: local, to: relay)
                  pump(from: relay, to: local)
                  return
              }
              tokenSent = true
              relay.send(content: token, completion: .contentProcessed { [weak self] error in
                  guard let self else { return }
                  if error == nil { self.advance() } else { self.stop() }
              })
          }
      
          private func pump(from source: NWConnection, to destination: NWConnection) {
              source.receive(minimumIncompleteLength: 1, maximumLength: 256 * 1024) {
                  [weak self] data, _, isComplete, error in
                  guard let self, !self.stopped else { return }
                  if let data, !data.isEmpty {
                      destination.send(content: data, completion: .contentProcessed { [weak self] sendError in
                          guard let self else { return }
                          if sendError == nil, !isComplete, error == nil {
                              self.pump(from: source, to: destination)
                          } else {
                              self.stop()
                          }
                      })
                      return
                  }
                  if isComplete || error != nil { self.stop(); return }
                  self.pump(from: source, to: destination)
              }
          }
      
          private func stop() {
              guard !stopped else { return }
              stopped = true
              local.cancel()
              relay.cancel()
              onStop?()
          }
      }
      //! The signalling conversation, as JSON over a WebSocket.
      //!
      //! This is the only place the two ends and the relay have to agree on a shape, and it is
      //! deliberately the smallest part of the system. Signalling carries no media — it introduces two
      //! parties and hands out the endpoints they will actually use. Once a session exists, nothing the
      //! relay says can affect what the two ends do with it, because every byte that matters is already

              video_token: String,

          Error { code: String, message: String },

      impl ServerMessage {
          pub fn error(code: &str, message: impl Into<String>) -> Self {

                  message: message.into(),

      /// Hex, because it needs no dependency, is trivially readable in a log, and these are 16 bytes that
      /// travel inside TLS.
      pub fn hex(bytes: &Token) -> String {
          use std::fmt::Write;
          bytes
              .iter()
              .fold(String::with_capacity(bytes.len() * 2), |mut out, b| {
                  let _ = write!(out, "{b:02x}");
                  out
              })

      pub fn unhex(text: &str) -> Option<Token> {
          if text.len() != 32 {
              return None;
          }
          let mut out = [0u8; 16];
          for (i, byte) in out.iter_mut().enumerate() {
              *byte = u8::from_str_radix(text.get(i * 2..i * 2 + 2)?, 16).ok()?;
          }
          Some(out)
      }

      //! Sessions: the pairing of one phone with one Mac, and the rendezvous that lets two connections
      //! that both travelled outbound find each other.
      //!
      //! **A session is an address, not an authorization.** Everything here exists to answer "which two
      //! endpoints belong together", and nothing here decides whether they are *allowed* to talk. That
      //! decision is made by the two ends themselves, in the TLS handshake and the pin that follows it,
      //! and it is the only reason this relay can be a dumb forwarder without being a security hole.
      //!
      //! A direct consequence, and one worth being explicit about: the control token is not a secret.
      //! It has to be presented in the clear before TLS starts, because TLS is what it is carrying. All
      //! it does is claim a place in a splice; someone who steals it gets a connection that fails its
      //! handshake.
      
      use std::collections::HashMap;
      use std::net::SocketAddr;
      use std::sync::Arc;
      use std::time::{Duration, Instant};
      
      use rand::Rng;
      use tokio::net::TcpStream;
      use tokio::sync::{oneshot, Mutex};
      
      /// A 128-bit addressing hint. See the module comment for what it is and is not.
      pub type Token = [u8; 16];
      
      pub fn new_token() -> Token {
          let mut token = [0u8; 16];
          rand::rng().fill(&mut token);
          token
      }
      
      /// What happened when a connection presented its control token.
      pub enum Join {
          /// First to arrive. This side keeps its own stream and waits for the peer's, so it ends up
          /// holding both halves and owns the splice.
          Waiting {
              mine: TcpStream,
              peer: oneshot::Receiver<TcpStream>,
          },
      
          /// Second to arrive. Our stream has been handed to the side that got here first, and this task
          /// is finished — the connection lives on in theirs.
          HandedOver,
      }
      
      /// The two control connections of a session, as they arrive.
      #[derive(Default)]
      struct ControlPairing {
          waiting: Option<oneshot::Sender<TcpStream>>,
      }
      
      /// The two video endpoints of a session, as they bind.
      ///
      /// **Each end holds a different token, and that is the whole design.** The obvious alternative — one
      /// shared token — cannot express what a bind packet needs to say. Both ends send the same thing, so
      /// the relay cannot tell which slot a re-bind belongs to, and a phone whose carrier NAT moved it
      /// mid-session would be indistinguishable from a stranger trying to take a slot. It would also make
      /// slot assignment depend on which packet happened to arrive first, so a log line saying "slot 0"
      /// would mean the phone or the Mac depending on timing. Two tokens make the mapping fixed: slot 0 is
      /// always the client, slot 1 is always the host, whoever gets there first.
      ///
      /// A `std::sync::Mutex` guards this rather than a tokio one because it is touched on the datagram
      /// path and nothing here awaits — a tokio mutex would add a queue for no reason.
      pub struct VideoPairing {
          /// Indexed by slot: 0 is the client, 1 is the host.
          tokens: [Token; 2],
          addrs: [Option<SocketAddr>; 2],
          last_activity: Option<Instant>,
      }
      
      /// Slot 0. The phone.
      pub const CLIENT_SLOT: usize = 0;
      /// Slot 1. The Mac.
      pub const HOST_SLOT: usize = 1;
      
      impl VideoPairing {
          pub fn new(tokens: [Token; 2]) -> Self {
              Self {
                  tokens,
                  addrs: [None, None],
                  last_activity: None,
              }
          }
      
          /// Claims the slot belonging to `token`, pointing it at `from`.
          ///
          /// Rebinding is the normal path, not an exception: each call simply replaces the address for
          /// that token's slot. A phone whose mapping moved re-sends its bind packet and is immediately
          /// reachable again — which is the one thing the video path has to survive that the control path
          /// does not, because control can reconnect and datagrams cannot.
          ///
          /// Returns `None` for a token that is not one of ours, so an address cannot be inserted into
          /// someone else's session.
          pub fn bind(&mut self, token: &Token, from: SocketAddr) -> Option<u8> {
              // Not a constant-time comparison, and it does not need to be: these tokens travel inside
              // TLS to their intended recipient and are addressing hints rather than credentials. See the
              // module comment.
              let slot = self.tokens.iter().position(|known| known == token)?;
              self.addrs[slot] = Some(from);
              self.last_activity = Some(Instant::now());
              Some(slot as u8)
          }
      
          /// Where a datagram from `from` should go, if both ends have bound.
          ///
          /// Returns `None` for an unknown source, which is also how a stolen or guessed address is
          /// handled: unbound addresses are dropped without a reply, so the relay never confirms that a
          /// session exists to someone who was not told about it.
          pub fn peer_of(&self, from: &SocketAddr) -> Option<SocketAddr> {
              let slot = self.slot_of(from)?;
              self.addrs[1 - slot as usize]
          }
      
          fn slot_of(&self, addr: &SocketAddr) -> Option<u8> {
              self.addrs
                  .iter()
                  .position(|slot| slot.as_ref() == Some(addr))
                  .map(|index| index as u8)
          }
      
          pub fn is_complete(&self) -> bool {
              self.addrs.iter().all(Option::is_some)
          }

          pub fn idle_for(&self) -> Duration {
              self.last_activity
                  .map(|at| at.elapsed())
                  .unwrap_or_default()
          }
      }

              let video_tokens = [new_token(), new_token()];

              // video task to stop and release the port. Nothing else has to be arranged.

                  control_token,
                  Session {
                      host_id: host_id.to_string(),
                      client_id: client_id.to_string(),
                      video_tokens,
                      control: ControlPairing::default(),
                      shutdown,
                      last_activity: Instant::now(),

                  control_token,
                  video_tokens,

          /// whoever is already waiting.
          pub async fn join_control(&self, token: &Token, mine: TcpStream) -> Option<Join> {

              // reason `Waiting` carries it back out: whoever waits has to splice, and splicing needs
              // both halves.
              let waiting = session.control.waiting.take();
              Some(match waiting {
                  Some(peer) => {
                      let _ = peer.send(mine);

                  None => {

                      session.control.waiting = Some(tx);
                      Join::Waiting { mine, peer: rx }

              })

                  .sessions
                  .retain(|_, session| session.last_activity.elapsed() < ttl);
              before - inner.sessions.len()

      ---
      name: diagnosing-bugs
      description: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.
      ---
      
      # Diagnosing Bugs
      
      A discipline for hard bugs. Skip phases only when explicitly justified.
      
      When exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) to get a clear mental model of the relevant modules, and check ADRs in the area you're touching.
      
      ## Redact
      
      This skill has you show commands, outputs and captured artifacts. **Redact every secret first**: write `<REDACTED>` in its place. Build loops against env vars, so the credential stays in the environment rather than in what you show. Captured artifacts carry auth headers: quote only the lines that carry the signal.
      
      If the redacted output is not enough to diagnose the bug, say so and ask the user.
      
      ## Phase 1: Build a feedback loop
      
      **This is the skill.** Everything else is mechanical. If you have a **tight** pass/fail signal for the bug (one that goes red on _this_ bug), you will find the cause; bisection, hypothesis-testing, and instrumentation all just consume it. If you don't have one, no amount of staring at code will save you.
      
      Spend disproportionate effort here. **Be aggressive. Be creative. Refuse to give up.**
      
      ### Ways to construct one, in roughly this order
      
      1. **Failing test** at whatever seam reaches the bug: unit, integration, e2e.
      2. **Curl / HTTP script** against a running dev server.
      3. **CLI invocation** with a fixture input, diffing stdout against a known-good snapshot.
      4. **Headless browser script** (Playwright / Puppeteer) that drives the UI and asserts on DOM/console/network.
      5. **Replay a captured trace.** Save a real network request / payload / event log to disk; replay it through the code path in isolation.
      6. **Throwaway harness.** Spin up a minimal subset of the system (one service, mocked deps) that exercises the bug code path with a single function call.
      7. **Property / fuzz loop.** If the bug is "sometimes wrong output", run 1000 random inputs and look for the failure mode.
      8. **Bisection harness.** If the bug appeared between two known states (commit, dataset, version), automate "boot at state X, check, repeat" so you can `git bisect run` it.
      9. **Differential loop.** Run the same input through old-version vs new-version (or two configs) and diff outputs.
      10. **HITL bash script.** Last resort. If a human must click, drive _them_ with `scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh` so the loop is still structured. Captured output feeds back to you.
      
      Build the right feedback loop, and the bug is 90% fixed.
      
      ### Tighten the loop
      
      Treat the loop as a product. Once you have _a_ loop, **tighten** it:
      
      - Can I make it faster? (Cache setup, skip unrelated init, narrow the test scope.)
      - Can I make the signal sharper? (Assert on the specific symptom, not "didn't crash".)
      - Can I make it more deterministic? (Pin time, seed RNG, isolate filesystem, freeze network.)
      
      A 30-second flaky loop is barely better than no loop; a 2-second deterministic one is tight, a debugging superpower.
      
      ### Non-deterministic bugs
      
      The goal is not a clean repro but a **higher reproduction rate**. Loop the trigger 100×, parallelise, add stress, narrow timing windows, inject sleeps. A 50%-flake bug is debuggable; 1% is not, so keep raising the rate until it's debuggable.
      
      ### When you genuinely cannot build a loop
      
      Stop and say so explicitly. List what you tried. Ask the user for: (a) access to whatever environment reproduces it, (b) a redacted captured artifact (HAR file, log dump, core dump, screen recording with timestamps), or (c) permission to add temporary production instrumentation. Do **not** proceed to hypothesise without a loop.
      
      ### Completion criterion: a tight loop that goes red
      
      Phase 1 is done when the loop is **tight** and **red-capable**: you can name **one command** (a script path, a test invocation, a curl) that you have **already run at least once** (show the invocation and its output, redacted), and that is:
      
      - [ ] **Red-capable**: it drives the actual bug code path and asserts the **user's exact symptom**, so it can go red on this bug and green once fixed. Not "runs without erroring"; it must be able to _catch this specific bug_.
      - [ ] **Deterministic**: same verdict every run (flaky bugs: a pinned, high reproduction rate, per above).
      - [ ] **Fast**: seconds, not minutes.
      - [ ] **Agent-runnable**: you can run it unattended; a human in the loop only via `scripts/hitl-loop.template.sh`.
      
      If you catch yourself reading code to build a theory before this command exists, **stop: jumping straight to a hypothesis is the exact failure this skill prevents.** No red-capable command, no Phase 2.
      
      ## Phase 2: Reproduce + minimise
      
      Run the loop. Watch it go red as the bug appears.
      
      Confirm:
      
      - [ ] The loop produces the failure mode the **user** described, not a different failure that happens to be nearby. Wrong bug = wrong fix.
      - [ ] The failure is reproducible across multiple runs (or, for non-deterministic bugs, reproducible at a high enough rate to debug against).
      - [ ] You have captured the exact symptom (error message, wrong output, slow timing) so later phases can verify the fix actually addresses it.
      
      ### Minimise
      
      Once it's red, shrink the repro to the **smallest scenario that still goes red**. Cut inputs, callers, config, data, and steps **one at a time**, re-running the loop after each cut, and keep only what's load-bearing for the failure.
      
      Why bother: a minimal repro shrinks the hypothesis space in Phase 3 (fewer moving parts left to suspect) and becomes the clean regression test in Phase 5.
      
      Done when **every remaining element is load-bearing**: removing any one of them makes the loop go green.
      
      Do not proceed until you have reproduced **and** minimised.
      
      ## Phase 3: Hypothesise
      
      Generate **3–5 ranked hypotheses** before testing any of them. Single-hypothesis generation anchors on the first plausible idea.
      
      Each hypothesis must be **falsifiable**: state the prediction it makes.
      
      > Format: "If <X> is the cause, then <changing Y> will make the bug disappear / <changing Z> will make it worse."
      
      If you cannot state the prediction, the hypothesis is a vibe: discard or sharpen it.
      
      **Show the ranked list to the user before testing.** They often have domain knowledge that re-ranks instantly ("we just deployed a change to #3"), or know hypotheses they've already ruled out. Cheap checkpoint, big time saver. Don't block on it; proceed with your ranking if the user is AFK.
      
      ## Phase 4: Instrument
      
      Each probe must map to a specific prediction from Phase 3. **Change one variable at a time.**
      
      Tool preference:
      
      1. **Debugger / REPL inspection** if the env supports it. One breakpoint beats ten logs.
      2. **Targeted logs** at the boundaries that distinguish hypotheses.
      3. Never "log everything and grep".
      
      **Tag every debug log** with a unique prefix, e.g. `[DEBUG-a4f2]`. Cleanup at the end becomes a single grep. Untagged logs survive; tagged logs die.
      
      **Perf branch.** For performance regressions, logs are usually wrong. Instead: establish a baseline measurement (timing harness, `performance.now()`, profiler, query plan), then bisect. Measure first, fix second.
      
      ## Phase 5: Fix + regression test
      
      Write the regression test **before the fix**, but only if there is a **correct seam** for it.
      
      A correct seam is one where the test exercises the **real bug pattern** as it occurs at the call site. If the only available seam is too shallow (single-caller test when the bug needs multiple callers, unit test that can't replicate the chain that triggered the bug), a regression test there gives false confidence.
      
      **If no correct seam exists, that itself is the finding.** Note it. The codebase architecture is preventing the bug from being locked down. Flag this for the next phase.
      
      If a correct seam exists:
      
      1. Turn the minimised repro into a failing test at that seam.
      2. Watch it fail.
      3. Apply the fix.
      4. Watch it pass.
      5. Re-run the Phase 1 feedback loop against the original (un-minimised) scenario.
      
      ## Phase 6: Cleanup
      
      Required before declaring done:
      
      - [ ] Original repro no longer reproduces (re-run the Phase 1 loop)
      - [ ] Regression test passes (or absence of seam is documented)
      - [ ] All `[DEBUG-...]` instrumentation removed (`grep` the prefix)
      - [ ] Throwaway prototypes deleted (or moved to a clearly-marked debug location)
      - [ ] The hypothesis that turned out correct is stated in the commit / PR message, so the next debugger learns

      # MacCast domain glossary
      
      ## Capture source
      
      Something the host can stream now: a display, a running application, or a window.
      
      ## Running application
      
      A user-facing application process that currently owns capturable content. It has a process
      identity and can therefore be selected as a capture source.
      
      ## Installed application
      
      A user-facing application available on the host but not currently running. It can be launched,
      but it is not a capture source until it becomes a running application.
      
      ## Application catalogue
      
      The host's current, user-facing list of running and installed applications. Background agents,
      menu extras, helper processes, and duplicate instances are not applications in this catalogue.

      import AVFoundation
      import CoreMedia
      import Foundation
      import RemoteCore
      import SwiftUI
      import os
      
      // `nonisolated`, because this file's whole point is to run off the main actor. Without it the
      // default isolation applies to file-scope globals too, and the renderer's queue cannot read it.
      private nonisolated let videoLog = Logger(subsystem: "pl.dmq.peering", category: "video")
      
      /// Decodes and displays the host's video stream.
      ///
      /// ## Why there is no `VTDecompressionSession` here
      ///
      /// The obvious design — build a `VTDecompressionSession`, decode into `CVPixelBuffer`s, and
      /// hand those to a layer — does the same work twice. `AVSampleBufferDisplayLayer` already
      /// owns a hardware decode session internally and is fed *compressed* samples, so adding a
      /// second session means decompressing on the CPU side of a buffer that is about to be handed
      /// to hardware anyway: extra memory, extra latency, and a second decoder to keep in sync with
      /// the parameter sets. The layer's `sampleBufferRenderer` is the only object that needs to
      /// know the stream exists.
      ///
      /// ## Threading
      ///
      /// `nonisolated`, and deliberately so. The app target compiles with
      /// `SWIFT_DEFAULT_ACTOR_ISOLATION = MainActor`, which would otherwise bind every one of these
      /// methods to the main actor — and enqueueing a 60 Hz video stream on the thread that is also
      /// laying out SwiftUI is how a client drops frames while showing 100% CPU. Every method here
      /// runs on ``queue``, and nothing touches the layer off it.
      nonisolated final class VideoRenderer: @unchecked Sendable {
          /// What the UI shows about the stream. Read under the lock, so it is safe from any actor.
          struct Snapshot: Sendable, Equatable {
              var hasConfig = false
              var pixelWidth = 0
              var pixelHeight = 0
              var codec: VideoCodec = .h264
              var framesEnqueued = 0
              var framesDropped = 0
              var awaitingKeyframe = true
              var lastError: String?
          }
      
          private let queue = DispatchQueue(label: "pl.dmq.peering.video", qos: .userInteractive)
          private let lock = NSLock()
      
          private var renderer: AVSampleBufferVideoRenderer?
          private var formatDescription: CMVideoFormatDescription?
          private var snapshot = Snapshot()
      
          // MARK: - Attachment
      
          /// Binds the layer this renderer draws into. Called once, from `makeUIView`.
          ///
          /// `AVSampleBufferDisplayLayer` is a `CALayer` and is not `Sendable`, so handing it to
          /// another queue is a transfer the compiler cannot check. It is marked as one deliberately
          /// rather than laundered through a box: this is the only place the layer crosses a thread
          /// boundary, nothing here touches the layer afterwards, and `sampleBufferRenderer` — the
          /// object that is actually used — is documented as safe to enqueue into from a background
          /// thread, which is what makes running the decode path off the main actor possible at all.
          func attach(_ layer: AVSampleBufferDisplayLayer) {
              nonisolated(unsafe) let layer = layer
              queue.async { [weak self] in
                  guard let self else { return }
                  // The renderer, not the layer. The layer's own `enqueue`/`flush` come from
                  // `AVQueuedSampleBufferRendering`, which is deprecated on this class; the modern
                  // surface is the `sampleBufferRenderer` it vends.
                  self.renderer = layer.sampleBufferRenderer
              }
          }
      
          // MARK: - Stream lifecycle
      
          /// Applies a new stream description and resets the decoder to match.
          ///
          /// Called once per stream and again on every source change. The parameter sets are
          /// **out of band in H.264** — they are not repeated on each keyframe — so a decoder that
          /// keeps the old format description after the host switches display decodes garbage, or
          /// nothing, until it happens to be recreated.
          func configure(_ config: VideoStreamConfig) {
              queue.async { [weak self] in
                  guard let self else { return }
      
                  guard let format = Self.makeFormatDescription(config) else {
                      videoLog.error("rejected a \(config.codec.rawValue, privacy: .public) stream config: the parameter sets did not form a format description")
                      // The decoder is deliberately left with *nothing* rather than with the previous
                      // stream's description. Returning here without clearing it — which is what this
                      // did — kept the old format description live, so frames for the new source went
                      // on being wrapped in the old one: a picture the host is no longer sending,
                      // decoded against parameter sets that do not describe it. `enqueue` drops
                      // everything while `formatDescription` is nil, so the client shows black and
                      // `lastError` explains why, which is the honest outcome for a stream that
                      // cannot be decoded.
                      self.renderer?.flush()
                      self.formatDescription = nil
                      self.lock.withLock {
                          self.snapshot.hasConfig = false
                          self.snapshot.awaitingKeyframe = true
                          self.snapshot.lastError = "Unusable parameter sets for \(config.codec.rawValue)"
                      }
                      return
                  }
      
                  self.formatDescription = format
                  // The old pictures are in the old format. Flushing before the new frames arrive
                  // is what stops the layer rendering a frame whose SPS it has already replaced.
                  self.renderer?.flush()
      
                  self.lock.withLock {
                      self.snapshot.hasConfig = true
                      self.snapshot.pixelWidth = config.pixelWidth
                      self.snapshot.pixelHeight = config.pixelHeight
                      self.snapshot.codec = config.codec
                      self.snapshot.awaitingKeyframe = true
                      self.snapshot.lastError = nil
                  }
                  videoLog.notice("stream configured: \(config.codec.rawValue, privacy: .public) \(config.pixelWidth)x\(config.pixelHeight) with \(config.parameterSets.count) parameter set(s)")
              }
          }
      
          /// Submits one compressed picture.
          func enqueue(_ frame: EncodedVideoFrame) {
              queue.async { [weak self] in
                  guard let self, let renderer = self.renderer, let format = self.formatDescription else {
                      return
                  }
      
                  // The decoder failing is reported on the renderer, not by a return value, and it
                  // is sticky: without a flush the layer refuses every later frame and the picture
                  // simply never comes back.
                  //
                  // **This runs before the keyframe gate below, and the order is the fix rather
                  // than a preference.** The flush discards every picture the decoder was holding,
                  // which invalidates the stream in exactly the way a new config does — so it has
                  // to re-arm the gate and then be judged by it. With the two the other way round,
                  // an inter frame arriving on a failed renderer passed a gate that had already
                  // been evaluated, fell through this branch, and was enqueued onto a renderer that
                  // had just been emptied — and the flag set two lines above was cleared again on
                  // the way out. The frame could not decode, the layer failed again, and the stream
                  // stayed broken while the log said it was waiting for a keyframe.
                  if renderer.status == .failed {
                      videoLog.notice("renderer failed; flushing and waiting for a keyframe")
                      renderer.flush()
                      self.lock.withLock {
                          self.snapshot.awaitingKeyframe = true
                          self.snapshot.lastError = renderer.error?.localizedDescription
                      }
                  }
      
                  // Until the first keyframe arrives there is nothing to decode against — the
                  // parameter sets describe the stream, not the picture, and H.264 prediction runs
                  // from the last keyframe. Feeding an inter frame here produces a decode error and
                  // a flushed renderer, which costs the frames that were about to work.
                  let awaitingKeyframe = self.lock.withLock { self.snapshot.awaitingKeyframe }
                  if awaitingKeyframe && !frame.isKeyframe {
                      self.lock.withLock { self.snapshot.framesDropped += 1 }
                      return
                  }
      
                  if !renderer.isReadyForMoreMediaData {
                      // Backpressure, from the renderer rather than the layer. A keyframe is the one
                      // frame worth flushing for: dropping it would extend the wait for a recovery
                      // point, whereas dropping an inter frame costs a single picture.
                      guard frame.isKeyframe else {
                          self.lock.withLock { self.snapshot.framesDropped += 1 }
                          return
                      }
                      renderer.flush()
                  }
      
                  guard let sample = Self.makeSampleBuffer(frame, format: format) else {
                      self.lock.withLock { self.snapshot.framesDropped += 1 }
                      return
                  }
      
                  renderer.enqueue(sample)
                  self.lock.withLock {
                      self.snapshot.framesEnqueued += 1
                      self.snapshot.awaitingKeyframe = false
                  }
              }
          }
      
          /// Drops the stream: the display goes black and the next frame must be a keyframe.
          func reset() {
              queue.async { [weak self] in
                  guard let self else { return }
                  self.renderer?.flush()
                  self.formatDescription = nil
                  self.lock.withLock {
                      self.snapshot = Snapshot()
                  }
              }
          }
      
          var currentSnapshot: Snapshot { lock.withLock { snapshot } }
      
          // MARK: - Format description
      
          /// Builds the description `CMSampleBufferCreateReady` needs, from the parameter sets the
          /// host sent out of band.
          ///
          /// `nalUnitHeaderLength: 4` is not a guess — it is what AVCC means, and it is the reason
          /// the frame payload can be handed over verbatim: both the format description and the
          /// sample data agree that each NALU is preceded by a 4-byte big-endian length.
          private static func makeFormatDescription(_ config: VideoStreamConfig) -> CMVideoFormatDescription? {
              // `NSData` rather than `Data` for the pointers: the API takes raw pointers that must
              // outlive the call, and `NSData` gives a stable `bytes` pointer plus a reference the
              // `withExtendedLifetime` below keeps alive. `Data.withUnsafeBytes` cannot be nested
              // across an array of values without the same dance, with more ways to get it wrong.
              var pointers: [UnsafePointer<UInt8>] = []
              var sizes: [Int] = []
              var storage: [NSData] = []
      
              for set in config.parameterSets where !set.isEmpty {
                  let data = set as NSData
                  guard let base = data.bytes.assumingMemoryBound(to: UInt8.self) as UnsafePointer<UInt8>? else {
                      continue
                  }
                  pointers.append(base)
                  sizes.append(data.length)
                  storage.append(data)
              }
              guard !pointers.isEmpty else { return nil }
      
              return withExtendedLifetime(storage) { () -> CMVideoFormatDescription? in
                  var format: CMVideoFormatDescription?
                  let status: OSStatus
      
                  switch config.codec {
                  case .h264:
                      status = CMVideoFormatDescriptionCreateFromH264ParameterSets(
                          allocator: kCFAllocatorDefault,
                          parameterSetCount: pointers.count,
                          parameterSetPointers: pointers,
                          parameterSetSizes: sizes,
                          nalUnitHeaderLength: 4,
                          formatDescriptionOut: &format
                      )
                  case .hevc:
                      status = CMVideoFormatDescriptionCreateFromHEVCParameterSets(
                          allocator: kCFAllocatorDefault,
                          parameterSetCount: pointers.count,
                          parameterSetPointers: pointers,
                          parameterSetSizes: sizes,
                          nalUnitHeaderLength: 4,
                          extensions: nil,
                          formatDescriptionOut: &format
                      )
                  }
      
                  guard status == noErr, let format else {
                      videoLog.error("format description creation failed with OSStatus \(status, privacy: .public)")
                      return nil
                  }
                  return format
              }
          }
      
          // MARK: - Sample buffers
      
          /// Wraps one AVCC payload in a `CMSampleBuffer` the renderer can decode.
          ///
          /// `decodeTimeStamp = .invalid` is correct here and is not a shortcut: the host encodes
          /// with `AllowFrameReordering = false`, so presentation order *is* decode order and there
          /// is no second timestamp to supply. Declaring one would make the layer wait for a
          /// reorder that never comes.
          private static func makeSampleBuffer(
              _ frame: EncodedVideoFrame,
              format: CMVideoFormatDescription
          ) -> CMSampleBuffer? {
              let length = frame.data.count
              guard length > 0 else { return nil }
      
              // A block buffer owning its own memory, then a copy in. The alternative — pointing at
              // the frame's bytes — would need the `Data` to outlive the sample buffer, which it
              // does not: the caller drops it the moment this returns.
              var blockBuffer: CMBlockBuffer?
              guard CMBlockBufferCreateWithMemoryBlock(
                  allocator: kCFAllocatorDefault,
                  memoryBlock: nil,
                  blockLength: length,
                  blockAllocator: kCFAllocatorDefault,
                  customBlockSource: nil,
                  offsetToData: 0,
                  dataLength: length,
                  flags: 0,
                  blockBufferOut: &blockBuffer
              ) == kCMBlockBufferNoErr, let blockBuffer else {
                  return nil
              }
      
              let copied = frame.data.withUnsafeBytes { raw -> OSStatus in
                  guard let base = raw.baseAddress else { return -1 }
                  return CMBlockBufferReplaceDataBytes(
                      with: base,
                      blockBuffer: blockBuffer,
                      offsetIntoDestination: 0,
                      dataLength: length
                  )
              }
              guard copied == kCMBlockBufferNoErr else { return nil }
      
              var timing = CMSampleTimingInfo(
                  duration: .invalid,
                  presentationTimeStamp: Self.time(from: frame.presentationTime),
                  decodeTimeStamp: .invalid
              )
              var sampleSize = length
              var sampleBuffer: CMSampleBuffer?
      
              guard CMSampleBufferCreateReady(
                  allocator: kCFAllocatorDefault,
                  dataBuffer: blockBuffer,
                  formatDescription: format,
                  sampleCount: 1,
                  sampleTimingEntryCount: 1,
                  sampleTimingArray: &timing,
                  sampleSizeEntryCount: 1,
                  sampleSizeArray: &sampleSize,
                  sampleBufferOut: &sampleBuffer
              ) == noErr, let sampleBuffer else {
                  return nil
              }
      
              // Without this the layer schedules the picture against the presentation timestamp and
              // holds it for a frame interval. For a remote desktop that is pure added latency: the
              // picture is already late by the time it arrives, and there is nothing to smooth.
              CMSetAttachment(
                  sampleBuffer,
                  key: kCMSampleAttachmentKey_DisplayImmediately,
                  value: kCFBooleanTrue,
                  attachmentMode: kCMAttachmentMode_ShouldPropagate
              )
      
              return sampleBuffer
          }
      
          private static func time(from timestamp: VideoTimestamp) -> CMTime {
              // A zero timescale is invalid to CoreMedia and arrives off the network, so it is
              // replaced rather than trusted. 600 is the conventional H.264 timescale.
              let timescale = timestamp.timescale > 0 ? timestamp.timescale : 600
              return CMTime(value: timestamp.value, timescale: CMTimeScale(timescale))

              }
      
              if !options.switchTargets.isEmpty {
                  try checkSourceSwitches(
                      options.switchTargets,
                      sent: switches,
                      snapshot: snapshot
                  )
              }
      
              log("VIDEO RECEIVE OK")
          }
      
          /// The summary, printed whether or not anything arrived.
          ///
          /// Printed before the failure is thrown, deliberately: the numbers are what make an
          /// empty window legible ("0 frames in 3.00s of a 3.00s window" is a different situation
          /// from "2 frames, then the connection died"), and they are the only record of a run
          /// whose outcome is a failure.
          static func reportVideoSummary(
              _ snapshot: VideoReceiver.Snapshot,
              elapsed: TimeInterval,
              window: TimeInterval
          ) {
              let average = snapshot.frames > 0 ? Double(snapshot.bytes) / Double(snapshot.frames) : 0
              log("""
                  video summary: \(snapshot.frames) frame(s), \(snapshot.keyframes) keyframe(s), \
                  \(snapshot.bytes) AVCC byte(s) total, \(Int(average.rounded())) byte(s) average
                  """)
      
              let rate = elapsed > 0 ? Double(snapshot.frames) / elapsed : 0
              log(String(
                  format: "video summary: %.2fs elapsed of a %.2fs window, %.1f frame(s)/s observed",
                  elapsed, window, rate
              ))
      
              if let first = snapshot.first, let last = snapshot.last {
                  log(String(
                      format: "video summary: pts %.3fs → %.3fs, span %.3fs",
                      first.seconds, last.seconds, last.seconds - first.seconds
                  ))
              } else {
                  log("video summary: no presentation timestamps — nothing was encoded")
              }
      
              if let config = snapshot.config {
                  let expected = config.codec == .h264 ? 2 : 3
                  var line = """
                      video summary: config \(config.pixelWidth)×\(config.pixelHeight) \
                      \(config.codec.rawValue), \(config.parameterSets.count) parameter set(s)
                      """
                  line += " (expected \(expected) for \(config.codec.rawValue))"
                  if snapshot.configUpdates > 0 {
                      line += ", plus \(snapshot.configUpdates) mid-stream update(s)"
                  }
                  log(line)
              } else {
                  log("video summary: no videoConfig arrived, so there is nothing a decoder could start from")
              }
          }
      
          /// Why an empty window is empty — as far as this side of the connection can tell.
          ///
          /// The distinction is available and worth drawing, because the two cases send the reader
          /// to different places. The host sends a config the moment a video client attaches, and
          /// it only attaches once capture has produced a format description — so a config that
          /// never arrived says the capture path never got that far, while a config that did
          /// arrive says capture was running and the encoder still produced nothing.
          static func noFramesMessage(
              _ snapshot: VideoReceiver.Snapshot,
              elapsed: TimeInterval
          ) -> String {
              let base = """
                  authorized, connected, but no frames arrived in \(formatSeconds(elapsed))s
                  """
      
              guard snapshot.config == nil else {
                  return """
      
              lock.lock()
              defer { lock.unlock() }
      
              guard let config = snapshot.config else {
                  recordFailureLocked("""
                      a video frame arrived before any videoConfig. The config carries the codec, the \
                      picture size, and the parameter sets — and AVCC keeps those out of band — so \
                      without it the client cannot build a format description and cannot decode this \
                      frame at all.
                      """)
                  return
              }
      
              guard frame.pixelWidth == config.pixelWidth, frame.pixelHeight == config.pixelHeight else {
                  recordFailureLocked("""
                      a frame is \(frame.pixelWidth)×\(frame.pixelHeight) but the config says \
                      \(config.pixelWidth)×\(config.pixelHeight). The client sizes its layer from the \
                      config, so the picture would be stretched or cropped.
                      """)
                  return
              }
      
              guard !expectedKeyframe || frame.isKeyframe else {
                  recordFailureLocked("""
                      the first frame of the stream is not a keyframe. A delta frame encodes only the \
                      difference from a picture the client never received, so its decoder has nothing \
                      to apply it to and shows nothing at all — the client joined mid-stream and needs \
                      a keyframe to start from.
                      """)
                  return
              }
      
              let pts = frame.presentationTime
              guard pts.timescale != 0 else {
                  recordFailureLocked("""
                      a frame carries a presentation timestamp with a zero timescale (value \
                      \(pts.value)). VideoTimestamp.seconds divides by it, so every frame would \
                      present at 0s and the client would have no timing information at all.
                      """)
                  return
              }
      
              if let last = snapshot.last, pts.seconds < last.seconds {
                  recordFailureLocked(String(
                      format: """
                          presentation timestamps go backwards: %.3fs after %.3fs. Frames arrive in \
                          presentation order, and a client that reorders or drops on a non-monotonic \
                          timestamp shows the wrong picture at the wrong time.
                          """,
                      pts.seconds, last.seconds
                  ))
                  return
              }
      
              snapshot.frames += 1
              if frame.isKeyframe { snapshot.keyframes += 1 }
              snapshot.bytes += frame.data.count
              if snapshot.first == nil { snapshot.first = pts }
              snapshot.last = pts
              expectedKeyframe = false
          }
      
          // MARK: - Outcomes
      
          /// The connection ended before the window did. The caller judges whether that was early.
          private func recordEnd(_ reason: String) {
              lock.lock()
              defer { lock.unlock() }
              // A window that ended because the caller closed the connection is not an end, and a
              // validation failure already explains the transport error that followed it.
              guard !stopped, snapshot.failure == nil, snapshot.endedAt == nil else { return }
              snapshot.endedAt = Date()
              snapshot.endReason = reason
          }

      #!/bin/bash
      # Build, sign, and run the probe client.
      #
      # The signing step is not optional housekeeping. macOS grants keychain access to a specific
      # code identity, and SwiftPM's default ad-hoc signature is derived from the build hash — so
      # an unsigned probe can use a key it created moments ago and then be locked out of it after
      # the next rebuild, with `errSecAuthFailed` and no indication of why. Signing with a stable
      # identity makes that key usable across rebuilds, which is what lets the probe test the
      # "already paired" path at all.
      #
      # usage: Tools/run-probe.sh [probe arguments]
      set -euo pipefail
      
      HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
      PROBE_DIR="$HERE/MacCastProbe"
      
      # Pick the signing identity **deterministically**, and pin it.
      #
      # This machine has more than one "Apple Development" identity, and `find-identity` does not
      # promise an order. Taking `head -1` therefore meant the probe could be signed with a
      # different identity from one run to the next — and since macOS grants keychain access to a
      # specific code identity, the probe's own stored key would come back "denied". Worse, the
      # denial surfaces as a *modal SecurityAgent prompt* rather than an error, so an unattended
      # run hangs forever instead of failing. Pinning the hash here makes the signature stable,
      # which is the whole precondition for the stored key staying usable.
      #
      # Override with PROBE_SIGNING_IDENTITY=<hash> when the pinned identity is unavailable.
      PINNED_IDENTITY="${PROBE_SIGNING_IDENTITY:-}"
      if [ -z "$PINNED_IDENTITY" ]; then
          PINNED_IDENTITY="$(security find-identity -v -p codesigning \
              | grep -oE '[0-9A-F]{40} "Apple Development: [^"]*"' \
              | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | head -1)"
      fi
      IDENTITY="$PINNED_IDENTITY"
      
      cd "$PROBE_DIR"
      swift build 2>&1 | grep -E "error:|warning: " || true
      
      BIN="$(swift build --show-bin-path)/MacCastProbe"
      
      if [ -n "$IDENTITY" ]; then
          codesign --force --sign "$IDENTITY" --identifier pl.dmq.maccast.probe "$BIN" 2>&1 \
              | grep -v "replacing existing signature" || true
      else
          echo "warning: no codesigning identity found; keychain access may be denied after rebuilds" >&2
      fi
      
      # Exec the binary directly rather than through `swift run`, which would re-sign it ad-hoc.
      exec "$BIN" "$@"

      //! Signalling: how a phone finds out where its Mac is, and how the two of them are handed a
      //! session to meet in.
      //!
      //! Presence falls out of the connection rather than being tracked separately. A Mac is online
      //! exactly while it holds a signalling WebSocket open, so there is no heartbeat to tune, no stale
      //! registration to expire, and no way for the roster to disagree with reality — when the socket
      //! closes, the host is gone, and the next phone that asks is told so.
      //!
      //! This is what replaces Bonjour across the internet. The TXT record's three fields — id, name and
      //! protocol version — are the same three that travel here, because they are the same three facts:
      //! who this Mac is, what it is called, and whether the two ends can speak to each other.
      
      use std::collections::HashMap;
      use std::net::SocketAddr;
      use std::sync::Arc;
      use std::time::Duration;
      
      use futures_util::{SinkExt, StreamExt};
      use tokio::io::{AsyncRead, AsyncWrite};
      use tokio::net::TcpListener;
      use tokio::sync::{mpsc, Mutex};
      use tokio_tungstenite::tungstenite::Message;
      use tracing::{debug, info, warn};
      
      use crate::protocol::{hex, ClientMessage, ServerMessage};
      use crate::session::{CLIENT_SLOT, HOST_SLOT, Registry, Token};
      use crate::udp_relay;
      
      /// How the relay describes itself to the two ends.
      #[derive(Clone)]
      pub struct Settings {
          /// The name clients should connect back to. `None` means "whatever address this client
          /// reached us on", which is right for a directly-addressed relay and needs no configuration
          /// for the loopback case.
          pub host: Option<String>,
          /// The control port **as clients reach it**, which need not be the port the relay binds. A host
          /// that forwards a port on a shared address picks both numbers, and only the outside one is
          /// reachable.
          pub public_control_port: u16,
          pub video_bind: SocketAddr,
          /// Where session video ports come from — see [`udp_relay::PortPool`].
          pub video_ports: Arc<udp_relay::PortPool>,
          /// The video port as clients reach it, for the same reason as `public_control_port`. Only
          /// meaningful with a single-port range: with several, each session gets its own port and there
          /// is no per-session mapping to express.
          pub public_video_port: Option<u16>,
          pub session_ttl: Duration,
      }
      
      /// The Macs that are currently registered, by device ID.
      #[derive(Clone, Default)]
      pub struct HostRegistry {
          inner: Arc<Mutex<HashMap<String, Host>>>,
      }
      
      struct Host {
          name: String,
          protocol_version: u16,
          /// The push channel for this Mac's signalling connection.
          tx: mpsc::Sender<ServerMessage>,
      }
      
      /// A host's registration, cloned out of the registry so the lock is not held while a session is
      /// allocated underneath it.
      struct HostRef {
          tx: mpsc::Sender<ServerMessage>,
          name: String,
          protocol_version: u16,
      }
      
      impl HostRegistry {
          pub fn new() -> Self {
              Self::default()
          }
      
          async fn put(&self, device_id: &str, name: String, version: u16, tx: mpsc::Sender<ServerMessage>) {
              self.inner.lock().await.insert(
                  device_id.to_string(),
                  Host {
                      name,
                      protocol_version: version,
                      tx,
                  },
              );
          }
      
          /// Removes a registration **only if this connection still owns it**.
          ///
          /// Without the ownership check, a Mac that reconnects — a laptop changing networks does this
          /// routinely — has its old socket close *after* the new one registered, and the cleanup for
          /// the old one would delete the new one's entry. The Mac would then be unreachable while
          /// believing it was online, which is the worst of both.
          async fn remove_if_ours(&self, device_id: &str, tx: &mpsc::Sender<ServerMessage>) {
              let mut inner = self.inner.lock().await;
              if inner
                  .get(device_id)
                  .is_some_and(|host| host.tx.same_channel(tx))
              {
                  inner.remove(device_id);
              }
          }
      
          async fn entry_for(&self, device_id: &str) -> Option<HostRef> {
              self.inner.lock().await.get(device_id).map(|host| HostRef {
                  tx: host.tx.clone(),
                  name: host.name.clone(),
                  protocol_version: host.protocol_version,
              })
          }
      
          pub async fn online_count(&self) -> usize {
              self.inner.lock().await.len()
          }
      }
      
      /// Accepts signalling connections. `tls` wraps each socket before the WebSocket handshake; without
      /// it the signalling channel is plaintext, which is only appropriate on loopback.
      pub async fn serve(
          listener: TcpListener,
          registry: Arc<Registry>,
          hosts: HostRegistry,
          settings: Settings,
          tls: Option<tokio_rustls::TlsAcceptor>,
      ) {
          info!(addr = %listener.local_addr().map(|a| a.to_string()).unwrap_or_default(), "signalling listening");
      
          loop {
              let (stream, peer) = match listener.accept().await {
                  Ok(pair) => pair,
                  Err(error) => {
                      warn!(%error, "signalling listener could not accept");
                      continue;
                  }
              };
      
              // The address this client reached us on is the one it can reach us on again, which is why
              // this is read from the accepted socket rather than from configuration.
              let relay_host = match (&settings.host, stream.local_addr()) {
                  (Some(configured), _) => configured.clone(),
                  (None, Ok(local)) => local.ip().to_string(),
                  (None, Err(_)) => "127.0.0.1".to_string(),
              };
      
              let registry = Arc::clone(&registry);
              let hosts = hosts.clone();
              let settings = settings.clone();
      
              match &tls {
                  Some(acceptor) => {
                      let acceptor = acceptor.clone();
                      tokio::spawn(async move {
                          match acceptor.accept(stream).await {
                              Ok(secured) => {
                                  handle(secured, peer, relay_host, registry, hosts, settings).await
                              }
                              Err(error) => debug!(%peer, %error, "signalling TLS handshake failed"),
                          }
                      });
                  }
                  None => {
                      tokio::spawn(async move {
                          handle(stream, peer, relay_host, registry, hosts, settings).await
                      });
                  }
              }
          }
      }
      
      async fn handle<S>(
          stream: S,
          peer: SocketAddr,
          relay_host: String,
          registry: Arc<Registry>,
          hosts: HostRegistry,
          settings: Settings,
      ) where
          S: AsyncRead + AsyncWrite + Unpin + Send + 'static,
      {
          let ws = match tokio_tungstenite::accept_async(stream).await {
              Ok(ws) => ws,
              Err(error) => {
                  debug!(%peer, %error, "websocket handshake failed");
                  return;
              }
          };
      
          let (mut sink, mut source) = ws.split();
      
          // Every outgoing message goes through here, including replies to the message being handled.
          // That is what lets the select below own `sink` exclusively: a reply written straight to the
          // sink from the read arm would need it borrowed in both arms at once.
          let (tx, mut rx) = mpsc::channel::<ServerMessage>(32);
          let mut registered_as: Option<String> = None;
      
          loop {
              tokio::select! {
                  incoming = source.next() => {
                      match incoming {
                          Some(Ok(Message::Text(text))) => {
                              let reply = match serde_json::from_str::<ClientMessage>(&text) {
                                  Ok(message) => {
                                      dispatch(message, &tx, &registry, &hosts, &settings, &relay_host, &mut registered_as).await
                                  }
                                  Err(error) => {
                                      debug!(%peer, %error, "unparseable signalling message");
                                      Some(ServerMessage::error("protocol", "unrecognised message"))
                                  }
                              };
                              if let Some(message) = reply {
                                  // A full channel here would mean 32 queued replies to a client that is
                                  // not reading, which is already a client we are about to drop.
                                  let _ = tx.send(message).await;
                              }
                          }
                          Some(Ok(Message::Close(_))) | None => break,
                          // Ping, Pong and Binary are not part of this conversation. tungstenite answers
                          // protocol-level pings itself, so there is nothing to do for them here.
                          Some(Ok(_)) => {}
                          Some(Err(error)) => {
                              debug!(%peer, %error, "signalling read failed");
                              break;
                          }
                      }
                  }
      
                  outgoing = rx.recv() => {
                      let Some(message) = outgoing else { break };
                      let Ok(json) = serde_json::to_string(&message) else { continue };
                      if sink.send(Message::Text(json.into())).await.is_err() {
                          break;
                      }
                  }
              }
          }
      
          if let Some(device_id) = registered_as {
              hosts.remove_if_ours(&device_id, &tx).await;
              info!(%device_id, "host went offline");
          }
      }
      
      /// Handles one client message, returning the reply to send back to *this* connection.
      async fn dispatch(
          message: ClientMessage,
          self_tx: &mpsc::Sender<ServerMessage>,
          registry: &Arc<Registry>,
          hosts: &HostRegistry,
          settings: &Settings,
          relay_host: &str,
          registered_as: &mut Option<String>,
      ) -> Option<ServerMessage> {
          match message {
              ClientMessage::RegisterHost {
                  device_id,
                  name,
                  protocol_version,
              } => {
                  hosts
                      .put(&device_id, name.clone(), protocol_version, self_tx.clone())
                      .await;
                  *registered_as = Some(device_id.clone());
                  info!(%device_id, %name, protocol_version, "host registered");
                  Some(ServerMessage::Registered {
                      session_ttl_seconds: settings.session_ttl.as_secs(),
                  })
              }
      
              ClientMessage::ConnectToHost {
                  host_id,
                  client_id,
                  protocol_version,
              } => {
                  let Some(host) = hosts.entry_for(&host_id).await else {
                      debug!(%host_id, "asked for a host that is not registered");
                      return Some(ServerMessage::HostOffline { device_id: host_id });
                  };
      
                  // Checked here so a mismatched pair is told before either end spends a round trip on a
                  // handshake that would fail anyway. The two ends check it again themselves — this is a
                  // courtesy, not the enforcement.
                  if host.protocol_version != protocol_version {
                      return Some(ServerMessage::error(
                          "version",
                          format!(
                              "host speaks v{}, client speaks v{protocol_version}",
                              host.protocol_version
                          ),
                      ));
                  }
      
                  let allocated = registry.allocate(&host_id, &client_id).await;
      
                  let video_port = match udp_relay::serve_session(
                      settings.video_bind,
                      Arc::clone(&settings.video_ports),
                      Arc::clone(&allocated.video),
                      allocated.shutdown,
                      settings.session_ttl,
                  )
                  .await

I found a separate relay bug while measuring: the Swift apps were sending signalling JSON as a binary WebSocket frame, but `peeringd` deliberately accepts JSON only as text frames. That is why the host stayed on “Connecting…”. I’m locking that down with a regression test before changing it. The five-second video lag is still a separate LAN-path issue and remains next.

      @Suite("Relay protocol")
      struct RelayProtocolTests {
          @Test("a Mac registration uses peeringd's public JSON contract")
          func hostRegistration() throws {

      /// One JSON-over-WebSocket signalling connection to `peeringd`.
      public final class RelaySignallingConnection: @unchecked Sendable {
          private let task: URLSessionWebSocketTask
      
          public init(url: URL, session: URLSession = .shared) {
              task = session.webSocketTask(with: url)
              task.resume()
          }
      
          public func send(_ message: RelayClientMessage) async throws {
              try await task.send(.data(try RelayMessageCodec.encode(message)))
          }
      
          public func receive() async throws -> RelayServerMessage {
              let data: Data
              switch try await task.receive() {
              case .data(let value): data = value
              case .string(let value): data = Data(value.utf8)
              @unknown default: throw RelaySignallingError.nonWebSocketResponse
              }
              return try RelayMessageCodec.decode(RelayServerMessage.self, from: data)
          }
      
          public func cancel() {
              task.cancel(with: .goingAway, reason: nil)
          }

A normal browser request may show 502 because this endpoint is WebSocket-only, but 502 can also mean nginx cannot reach `peeringd`. I’m checking both the ordinary HTTPS response and an actual WebSocket upgrade so we can tell which it is.

      /// framing layer is the only place that has to care.

                  case .cancelled:
                      finish(nil)
